#7821. Florida Ban on Material Support to "Domestic Terrorist Organizations" Can't Be Applied to Legal Advice to CAIR

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From CAIR-Foundation, Inc. v. DeSantis Wednesday by Chief Judge Allen Winsor (N.D. Fla.):

The Florida Legislature recently enacted a new law that allows state officials to designate certain groups "domestic terrorist organizations" (DTOs). Soon thereafter, Florida's Governor and Cabinet designated Plaintiffs CAIR-Foundation, Inc., and CAIR-Florida, Inc., as DTOs. The designations take effect on November 5, 2026. At that point, Plaintiffs and others supporting them will be subject to criminal and civil penalties for certain activities. In this action, Plaintiffs contend the new law (or parts of it) and the DTO designations violate their First Amendment freedoms and due process protections….

This is Florida's second effort to designate Plaintiffs as terrorist organizations. Previously, the Governor issued an executive order that designated Plaintiffs as terrorist organizations and prevented them "or 'any person known to have provided material support or resources' to [them] 'from receiving any contract, employment, funds, or other benefit or privilege' from executive or cabinet agencies or from any county or municipality of the state." This court preliminarily enjoined enforcement of the executive order, finding it likely violates the First Amendment. [See this post on that decision. -EV] The Governor appealed, and the appeal remains pending.

After this court's decision, the Florida Legislature enacted HBs 1471 and 1473, which created a DTO designation process. The Florida Department of Law Enforcement later promulgated Emergency Rule 11RER26-8, which implements this legislation. Pursuant to the legislation and rule, Florida's Chief of Domestic Security issued a written notice of intent to designate Plaintiffs as DTOs…. [T]he Governor and Cabinet held a public meeting, at which they approved the designations….

{[U]nder [Fla. Stat.] § 775.33(3), "[a] person who knowingly provides material support or resources to a designated … domestic terrorist organization" commits a first-degree felony. See also Fla. Stat. § 775.33(1)(d) ("'Material support or resources' means any property, tangible or intangible, or service, including currency or monetary instruments or financial securities, financial services, lodging, training, expert advice or assistance, safe houses, false documentation or identification, communications equipment, facilities, weapons, lethal substances, explosives, personnel, or transportation. The term does not include medicine or religious materials.").}

A few preliminary points are in order. First, much of Plaintiffs' case is not at issue at this stage. Plaintiffs allege that state officials sought to punish them for their earlier speech and for their religious views. They have a First Amendment retaliation claim, but they did not move for preliminary injunctive relief based on that claim. They also have a preemption claim that is not yet at issue….

[Second], the issue at this stage is not whether Plaintiffs are, in fact, terrorist organizations…. Plaintiffs say "[t]heir shared mission, rooted in faith, is to enhance the public's understanding of Islam, protect civil rights, promote justice, and empower American Muslims." Defendants, on the other hand, say Plaintiffs operate as fronts for Hamas and the Muslim Brotherhood. Again, Plaintiffs claim the State reached the wrong decision on that score—and that it violated their Fourteenth Amendment rights in reaching its decision without providing due process. But Plaintiffs do not assert any standalone constitutional right to a factually correct decision on the question of whether they are terrorist organizations.

[Third], an entity's designation as a terrorist organization is indeed consequential. Plaintiffs have shown that the designations, upon taking effect, will cause significant disruption, essentially leading to a closure of all their Florida operations. Because one Plaintiff (CAIR Florida, Inc.) operates exclusively in Florida, it says it will shut down entirely. At this stage, based on undisputed statements in Plaintiffs' declarations, I accept these representations as true.

But while the designations and the state laws that authorize them may have broad implications, the constitutional issues Plaintiffs present are relatively narrow. The claims ask whether Plaintiffs were afforded due process before the State made the designations and whether the designations (and legal consequences flowing from them) violate Plaintiffs' speech or association rights….

The court rejected plaintiffs' due process claims, largely on the grounds that state law offered enough process for determining whether an entity indeed qualified as a DTO, including "[t]he availability of [a] state-court appeal" (something plaintiffs didn't take advantage of). The court also rejected their right to association claims, reasoning in part:

[The] prohibition against "knowingly provid[ing] material support or resources to a designated … domestic terrorist organization" … targets material support of DTOs—not their associations. As Defendants argue, Arcara v. Cloud Books, Inc. (1986), is instructive. In that case, the Supreme Court upheld enforcement of a civil statute that authorized the forced closure of a business used for prostitution and lewdness—but also used to sell adult books. The closed business argued "that the effect of the statutory closure remedy impermissibly burden[ed] its First Amendment protected bookselling activities." But that "argument prove[d] too much, since every civil and criminal remedy imposes some conceivable burden on First Amendment protected activities." Indeed, "[o]ne liable for a civil damages award has less money to spend on paid political announcements or to contribute to political causes," and "a thief who is sent to prison might complain that his First Amendment right to speak in public places has been infringed because of the confinement." The same principle applies here.

{There is some overlap between Plaintiffs' association claim and their content-based speech regulation claim. As explained below, Plaintiffs have shown a likelihood of success as to the content-based claim to the extent the statute precludes their continued use of legal counsel based on the "expert advice" provision. Arguably, that same restriction would violate Plaintiffs' association rights by precluding their association with counsel.

But Plaintiffs did not focus on legal advice in the section of their motion addressing their association claim. This makes some sense, as the arguments about counsel fit more neatly within Plaintiffs' content-based [speech restriction] claim than their broader association claim. For these reasons—and because, as a practical matter, the same limited injunction would issue—I choose at this preliminary stage not to further explore any distinction between these speech and association claims as to the "expert advice" restriction.}

The court also rejected the argument that DTO status automatically causes an organization to be treated as a "criminal gang" and thus subject to various criminal penalties. But the court held that the DTO regime's material support prohibition was likely unconstitutional, at least as to provision of material support in the form of legal advice:

[M]ost of what constitutes "[m]aterial support or resources" under Florida law is not speech:

"Material support or resources" means any property, tangible or intangible, or service, including currency or monetary instruments or financial securities, financial services, lodging, training, expert advice or assistance, safe houses, false documentation or identification, communications equipment, facilities, weapons, lethal substances, explosives, personnel, or transportation. The term does not include medicine or religious materials.

But the law expressly covers things that are speech, namely providing "expert advice," which includes legal advice. Plaintiffs argue this provision would preclude them from receiving their own lawyers' services in furtherance of this litigation, and Defendants have not shown otherwise.

As the parties note, the emergency rule includes this provision:

The Department will not consider there to be cause for prosecution for a violation of section 775.33 or Chapter 874, F.S., based solely on the provision of legal counsel or legal support services to the organization for purposes of representing or providing advice in connection with existing or anticipated litigation concerning a designation or defending against a criminal prosecution.

That does not preclude relief here for several reasons. One, it says what the [Florida Department of Law Enforcement] (FDLE) considers to be the case; it does not purport to bind the twenty State Attorneys or the Attorney General. Two, the rule does not cover Plaintiffs' providing support to each other in connection with the litigation—or any other third party or employee who might provide "expert advice" in connection with the litigation. And three, it purports only to cover limited types of cases—those in connection with litigation "concerning a designation" or related to criminal prosecutions. It would not, for example, cover the provision of legal services in connection with the pending Eleventh Circuit appeal in CAIR I.

Therefore, to the extent § 775.33(3) restricts interactions with counsel or others in support of litigation, it regulates speech based on content and is therefore subject to strict scrutiny. Strict scrutiny is a difficult standard to satisfy, and Defendants have not done so here. Defendants argue in a footnote that "[t]he designation statute creates a scheme of judicial review and thus cannot plausibly be construed to authorize the prosecution of CAIR employees who participate in judicial review." But even assuming that this purposivist interpretation is correct, the law still would not authorize employees or outside counsel to assist in this litigation—or any litigation other than the statutory appeal Plaintiffs have not taken.

In arguing that the law can survive strict-scrutiny review, Defendants say "combatting terrorism is a textbook compelling interest." Even so, Defendants must show that their restriction—here, precluding Plaintiffs from using or employing legal counsel for any purpose (save, perhaps, for the statutory appeal Plaintiffs do not pursue)—is the least restrictive means available to advance that interest. They have not done so. Indeed, their assertion that the law allows Plaintiffs to use legal counsel to preserve their non-designation status through one form of litigation (the statutory appeal) only undermines any suggestion that prohibiting Plaintiffs from using counsel to preserve that status through another form of litigation (this case) is the least restrictive means.

Defendants rely heavily on Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project, which upheld a federal material-support statute against a First Amendment challenge. But in that case, the Court relied in large part on the federal interest in addressing international terrorism. The Court declined to "suggest that Congress could extend the same prohibition on material support … to domestic organizations." It also did not hold that the government could preclude the organizations from employing legal counsel to assist them in the litigation.

The bottom line is that the challenged law does, in some respects, restrict speech based on content. It criminalizes any third party's (including counsel's) providing "expert advice"—of any kind—to Plaintiffs. It thus restricts Plaintiffs' First Amendment right to receive such speech. See Stanley v. Georgia (1969) (noting that the First Amendment protects the right to receive speech just as it protects the right to make speech).

Aside from litigation activity, however, Plaintiffs do not offer specificity as to any other "expert advice" they wish to receive that § 775.33(3) would arguably criminalize. Thus, I agree with Defendants that much of Plaintiffs' argument is hypothetical. There was some discussion at the hearing regarding "training," which also could constitute speech the law would prohibit, but Plaintiffs have not advanced any specific argument regarding training they wish to receive. The relief available is a product of Plaintiffs' litigation choices. Cf. Holder (evaluating "the particular speech plaintiffs propose to undertake" and noting that "future applications of the material-support statute to speech or advocacy [may not] survive First Amendment scrutiny").

Still, Plaintiffs have shown it likely they will succeed in proving the "expert advice" restriction as applied to their receipt of legal services violates their First Amendment rights. As to all other claims, they have not shown a likelihood of success on the merits….

NEXT: Senator-Governor Klobuchar and the Problem of the Received Wisdom

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. #7820. 5 Annual Flowers I Bring Indoors to Brighten Winter

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 5, 2026 10:34 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

I like to grow exotic species indoors for flowering during the winter months, either under grow lights or on a sunny windowsill. However, I also save a few annuals from my garden, usually container types that don’t require large amounts of light to flourish. After all, annuals are easy to bring into flowering, while some tropicals and other perennials can be challenging to coax into bloom.

Plants like geraniums (Pelargonium spp.) and flowering maples (Abutilon spp.) can be long-blooming indoor annual flowers. In addition, the annuals listed below can often bloom longer indoors, extending the life of your annual flowers and brightening rooms in winter.

Although I bring tuberous begonias indoors over winter, I always let them die back to their tubers, since they require a period of dormancy to bloom well the following summer. However, I’ve found that other begonia species such as the wax begonia (B. semperflorens) will flower cheerfully almost year-round. After all, its species name means “ever-blooming.”

I’ve learned to be careful not to overwater the plants during winter as I have had favorites, including the double-flowered cultivar pictured above, succumb to root rot. But otherwise, wax begonias are easy-care plants that can add indoor winter color.

Common impatiens (Impatiens walleriana) plants flower busily both outdoors and indoors. Because they root easily in water, I often take cuttings of them in late summer to pot up later, but sometimes just prune back a mature plant to bring inside.

The semidouble type of Busy Lizzy is seldom available in my area, so I saved one of my I. walleriana ‘Athena’ plants last autumn, and it continued to perform under the lights over winter and in the container pictured in the banner image this summer. I’ve occasionally also grown more unusual cultivars of impatiens under lights, including Giant Balsam (I. grandis, pictured above) and rare species such as Blue Diamond Impatiens (I. namchabarwensis).

Coleus cuttings also root quickly in water. That’s a good thing because the Big Bad Boys cultivar I grew this summer lived up to its name by eventually growing to 2 feet, even when packed into a container with other shade-loving annuals. So, I will need to take cuttings or prune the plant to restore it to a suitable size for grow lights.

Since coleus annuals, such as the blazingly red type above, are grown for their boldly colored foliage rather than their nondescript blooms, I usually try to pinch out any bud stalks that sprout. Otherwise, these are easy-care indoor annual flowers.

Due to their preference for cool and somewhat humid conditions, fuchsias often do well under my basement grow lights. And, yes, their cuttings, too, will root easily in water should you not want to bring an entire hanging basket indoors.

As with most annuals, fuchsias won’t bloom as heavily in the house as they do outside, but they will make some flowers. I believe those pictured—blooming under lights one late December—are the elegantly elongated Bolivian fuchsia (F. boliviana). But the typical hanging basket type called Lady’s Eardrops (F. magellanica) also will perform as indoor winter plants under the right conditions.

I have a very old Lantana camara plant with a large, gnarled and knotted trunk that looks more like a bonsai specimen than a potted annual. But it proves that lantanas, also called shrub verbenas, can last almost indefinitely if protected during winter. In fact, they can be perennial plants in warm growing zones.(7 to 11).

However, I’ve found that my plant will drop most of its leaves after being brought indoors. It isn’t dying, just adapting to new light levels. It might qualify as one of the fragrant indoor plants since its leaves have a peculiar odor that some people compare to citrus and others to gasoline.

Because my windows are drafty and don’t receive much illumination during winter, I place most of my flowering indoor plants under grow lights, either fluorescent or LED. (I am gradually switching over to the latter, since they make more light while using less energy.)

I use 4-foot fixtures and keep most of the plants in the basement, where conditions are cooler and more humid than in the rest of the house. Since some of my plants require short days to bloom, I keep the lights on timers so they are on for no more than 12 hours per day.

These full-spectrum grow light panels are lightweight and low-heat, making them our top pick for boosting indoor plants during winter.

One problem with having tropical plants and other flowering annuals in the basement is that out of sight often means out of mind. So, I have to remember to trudge down the stairs with a watering can at least once per day. Since it is easy to accidentally overwater plants in winter, I test the surface of their soil with a fingertip first and only water when that surface is dry.

If a plant is blooming, I often bring it upstairs to enjoy before returning it to its original position under the lights. That is my way of feeding my flower addiction during winter.

All You Need to Care for Your Lawn & Garden

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

Black-eyed Susan (Rudbeckia spp.) is a popular native perennial, loved for its cheerful, daisy-like flowers with bright yellow petals and contrasting dark centers. As a native flower, this perennial is generally easy to grow, especially once established in the right conditions

One aspect of black-eyed Susan care that can be confusing for gardeners is pruning. Should you deadhead the flowers? Should you cut plants back all the way in winter? How do you trim black-eyed Susans? The answers to these questions, and more, depend on your goals, the time of year, and the types of Rudbeckia.

In our expert guide, we explain when and how to trim and prune black-eyed Susan and answer gardeners’ most frequently asked questions. Careful and timely pruning will keep your plants healthy and coming back year after year.

The timing for pruning black-eyed Susan depends on the reason for doing so. There are a few opportunities throughout the year:

Even within these parameters, gardeners have some wiggle room. You don’t have to deadhead, for instance. You also don’t have to cut back healthy plants just because the growing season has come to an end.

Exactly how you’ll cut back your plants depends on the specific task, but these are general best practices for routine pruning:

Trim off any diseased-looking plant material whenever you see it and dispose of it in the waste, not compost.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Deadheading is one of the most useful pruning chores gardeners have at their disposal. Selective removal of spent flowers keeps perennials like black-eyed Susans flowering until seasonal and weather changes start to trigger dormancy.

Remove spent flowers once the petals fade and drop off, or whenever they no longer look tidy or at their peak. Cut the stem under the flower back to the next healthy leaf or side bud.

You can also accompany summer deadheading with a light overall trim if the plant is looking leggy. Trim stems back to side buds or the base, but do so carefully and selectively. Avoid heavy pruning in summer.

As long as the plant looks healthy, you can keep your black-eyed Susan standing in fall and through winter. The standing seedheads provide valuable food for birds in winter and offer some visual interest in winter beds. The plants also provide shelter for beneficial insects.

If your plants don’t look healthy, for instance if you see signs of fungal disease, it’s best to cut them back. Cut all the stems and foliage back to the ground and dispose of it. Don’t put it in the compost pile, as this can spread disease.

You can also cut back plants if you prefer a tidier appearance in winter. This can also help you prevent self-seeding if you don’t want your black-eyed Susans to spread.

Pruning needs are generally similar across types, but there are a few considerations for different black-eyed Susans:

Deadheading black-eyed Susans encourages more blooming in the same season. Severely cutting back the plant before it has gone dormant can reduce blooming. Cutting back before winter will not restrict next year’s flowers.

For deadheading, cut back to the next healthy leaf or side bud. For seasonal cut-backs, trim stems all the way down to the ground.

Deadheading is optional, but plants should be cut back all the way either in late fall before winter or in spring before or just as new growth emerges.

Not necessarily. Leaving native perennials in place over winter supports wildlife and offers some visual interest in garden beds. The exception is diseased plants. These should be cut back.

Black-eyed Susan pruning is actually pretty simple. Deadhead in summer to enjoy more flowers and cut back spent material before winter or in early spring. The choice is yours and depends on your preferences, type of plant, and whether or not you support native wildlife.

#7817. Lawsuit Against New York AG Letitia James over Letter Alleging Group's Event Was Connected to "White Nationalist Ideals" …

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

can go forward on First Amendment coercion, First Amendment retaliation, and defamation grounds, a federal district court concludes.

From Magistrate Judge Kenneth Schroeder's Report and Recommendation Sept. 22 in Doyle v. James, affirmed Wednesday by Judge John Sinatra (W.D.N.Y.), plaintiff's allegations:

Plaintiff Paul Doyle ("Doyle") is the Senior Pastor at Cornerstone Church in Batavia, New York. Cornerstone is a small, rural church with a history of service and community outreach. Cornerstone has worked to build relationships with communities of color and was aggressive in their assistance to victims of the mass shooting in Buffalo.

Plaintiff Clay Clark ("Clark") is the owner and operator of The Thrive Time Show, a highly successful business podcast. Clark has twice been named the US Small Business Association Entrepreneur of the Year and is the recipient of other business awards.

"ReAwaken America" is a conservative political movement that hosts events throughout the country. The ReAwaken America Tour ("the Tour") was scheduled to host an event in Rochester, New York on August 12, 2022 at the Main Street Armory. However, after community members and local politicians spoke out against the event, the Armory cancelled it.

The Tour then reached out to Doyle to see if Cornerstone would be willing to host the event. Doyle met with groups from Rochester to try to understand their concerns and concluded that "the Tour was not what was being portrayed in the media and by government officials." Doyle thus agreed to host the event at Cornerstone "due to his strong belief that free speech should not be restricted and those who attempt to exercise it should not be intimidated, particularly by government officials." The event was scheduled for August 11-13, 2022.

On August 3, 2022, New York Attorney General Letitia James sent a letter addressed to Clark and General Michael Flynn—a co-organizer of the Tour—to Doyle's home address "c/o Cornerstone Church." Plaintiffs allege that the letter was "nothing less than an attempt to covertly intimidate and threaten the Plaintiffs into shutting down the event."

As New York's top law enforcement officer, I have significant concerns that the ReAwaken America Tour's upcoming event at the Cornerstone Church in Batavia, New York on August 12 and 13 could spur extremist or racially motivated violence. These concerns center around the event's proposed dates, which coincide with the five-year anniversary of the deadly Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, and past extremist statements made by yourselves and the other featured speakers on the tour.

I am especially concerned about featured speakers' regular allusions to white nationalist ideals connected to the "Great Replacement Theory," a conspiracy theory that warns of white genocide and efforts to replace native born Americans with immigrants. The theory is frequently linked to violent actions, including the racially motivated mass shooting that killed 10 people at a Tops Friendly Markets store in Buffalo. Especially in light of this racist mass shooting, and other recent episodes of racially motivated violence in New York and throughout the country, the Office of the Attorney General is concerned that such rhetoric could contribute to violent or unlawful conduct at the ReAwaken America Tour's upcoming event….

The Office of the Attorney General writes to remind you that New York law prohibits racially motivated violence, harassment, or interference with another person in the exercise of their civil rights. New York Civil Rights Law § 79-n empowers the Office of the Attorney General to investigate acts of violence, intimidation, threats, or harassment directed at people based on a belief or perception regarding an individual's race, color, national origin, ancestry, gender, religion, religious practice, age, disability, or sexual orientation. In addition to actual damages, any person who violates this statute can be held liable for $5,000 in penalties for each violation.

Additionally, New York Civil Rights Law § 40-c prohibits discriminating against another person in the exercise of their civil rights—including their right to peacefully protest—based on similar protected characteristics. Finally, New York Executive Law § 63(12) empowers the Office of the Attorney General to take action against any business engaged in significant fraud or illegality—including the violation of New York's civil rights laws.

The Office of the Attorney General has a duty to protect New Yorkers from extremist and racially motivated violence. We stand ready to investigate any violation of the laws above and, if necessary, to enforce them to the fullest extent available. You are therefore instructed to take all necessary steps to ensure that the event complies fully with the requirements of New York's civil rights laws and all other applicable state and federal statutes.

Your cooperation in ensuring a peaceful and law-abiding event will be greatly appreciated.

Plaintiffs allege that James's "inferences towards racial discrimination and fraud associated with the church and the event were publicized in numerous media outlets … which injured Pastor Doyle's reputation, that of his church, and the reputation of Mr. Clark as well." They further allege that James made no reasonable inquiry to verify her alleged concerns and that, had she done so, she would have learned "about the generous history of Cornerstone Church, the upstanding reputation of both Plaintiffs, and the fact that the Reawaken America Tour had not a single publicized act of violence at any of their events, nor has the tour been legitimately accused of any crimes, illicit behavior, or the violation of any laws or ordinances." Plaintiffs also allege that they had "reached out to law enforcement and local government officials to ensure the safety of the event and that all local rules, laws, and ordinances would be followed."

Plaintiffs further allege that no ReAwaken America event has ever been associated with the racial theories or violence with which James's letter purported to connect them, and her statements were "negligent, reckless and a dereliction of her duty to exercise due diligence in her representation as Attorney General and in doing so, is an abuse of power."

Plaintiffs allege that James's politically motivated letter created a "smear" on their names and damaged their community relationships. The publicity surrounding James's letter resulted in "numerous cancellations of ticket sales by patrons who originally planned to attend the event prior to hearing the derisive false reports."

Finally, plaintiffs allege that, as a result, they were forced to hire additional security to ensure the safety of the participants and attendees. Ultimately, the event "went off without a single issue." …

The court held that plaintiffs had adequately alleged the letter was unconstitutionally coercive:

To state a claim that the government violated the First Amendment through coercion, "a plaintiff must plausibly allege conduct that, viewed in context, could be reasonably understood to convey a threat of adverse government action in order to punish or suppress the plaintiff's speech." …

Here, after linking plaintiffs and the event's speakers to racist theories and past incidents of racist violence, defendant listed various state anti-discrimination laws and their penalties, concluding that her office "stand[s] ready to investigate any violation of the laws above and, if necessary, to enforce them to the fullest extent available." Plaintiffs allege that they perceived this letter as a thinly veiled threat meant to cause them to cancel the event, accompanied by the specter of prosecution.

As this Court stated in its prior RR&O [Report, Recommendations & Order]:

Here, defendant's letter has a heavy-handed, ominous tone and tells plaintiffs that: (1) she considers their own past statements concerning and "extremist," (2) she believes that "such rhetoric" could lead to "violent or unlawful conduct" at the upcoming event; and (3) she "stands ready" to investigate and enforce violations of New York laws, whose penalties she enumerates.

Such statements might reasonably be understood as threats as opposed to a government official's speech that is "nothing more than a well-reasoned and sincere entreaty in support of his own political perspective." …

[D]efendant's assertion that her letter can only be construed to convey a request to avoid or prevent unlawful conduct is unavailing at the pleading stage. In NRA v. Vullo (2024), the Supreme Court rejected such an argument:

For the same reasons, this Court cannot simply credit Vullo's assertion that "pursuing conceded violations of the law …is an obvious alternative explanation" for her actions that defeats the plausibility of any coercive threat raising First Amendment concerns… Of course, discovery in this case might show that the allegations of coercion are false, or that certain actions should be understood differently in light of newly disclosed evidence. At this stage, though, the Court must assume the well-pleaded factual allegations in the complaint are true.

Given this context, the fact that defendant's letter did not cause plaintiffs to cancel their event does not preclude a finding that defendant's letter was an unlawful attempt to coerce them to do so. See Okwedy v. Molinari (2d Cir. 2003) ("A public-official defendant who threatens to employ coercive state power to stifle protected speech violates a plaintiff's First Amendment rights.")…. Therefore, construing the allegations of the complaint in plaintiffs' favor, and considering the above authorities, the Court concludes that plaintiffs have plausibly alleged that they "reasonably understood" defendant's letter to be an attempt to suppress the exercise of their First Amendment rights. Bantam Books, Inc. v. Sullivan (1963).

The court also held that plaintiffs had adequately alleged the letter was unconstitutionally retaliatory:

"Where a private plaintiff sues public officials, the Second Circuit states the elements [of a retaliation claim] as follows: (1) Plaintiffs have a right protected by the First Amendment; (2) Defendants' actions were motivated or substantially caused by Plaintiffs' exercise of that right; and (3) Defendants' actions caused Plaintiffs some injury." … [D]efendant does not contest that plaintiffs satisfy the first element of a retaliation claim…. [And] plaintiffs' complaint alleges facts which, construed as true, would allow a reasonable person to infer that defendant was motivated to send her letter due to the political content of plaintiffs' speech ….

[D]efendant argues that plaintiffs fail to adequately plead that defendant's actions caused them legally cognizable harm. The Court discussed the issue of harm in its prior RR&O in the context of standing, noting that "[v]arious non-speech related harms are sufficient to give a plaintiff standing" for purposes of a First Amendment retaliation claim. In particular, the Court reviewed authority holding that "reputational harms" may constitute such an injury. The Court observed:

Here, plaintiffs' complaint is replete with allegations that defendant's letter falsely associated them with racist, "white nationalist ideals;" the "Great Replacement Theory;" a racially motivated shooting in Buffalo, New York; and other "racially motivated violence." Plaintiffs allege specific damages flowing from defendant's statements: injury to plaintiffs' reputations; harm to Doyle's community relationships, and specifically with communities of color; and an increased likelihood of violence towards plaintiffs….

Thus, construing the above allegations in plaintiffs' favor, the Court concludes that they have sufficiently alleged injury for purposes of their retaliation claim….

The magistrate judge also concluded that the law was sufficiently well-established that it recommended denying qualified immunity to the defendants. An excerpt:

[I]t has long been clearly established that "implied threats to employ coercive state power to stifle protected speech" violate the First Amendment. Hammerhead Enters., Inc. v. Brezenoff (2d Cir. 1983).

In 2003, the Court of Appeals reversed the dismissal of a complaint filed by plaintiffs against the Borough President of Staten Island who sent a letter to a billboard company with whom plaintiffs had contracted to produce and display billboards conveying plaintiffs' beliefs that, under biblical teachings, homosexuality is a sin. Okwedy v. Molinari (2d Cir. 2003). The letter stated that defendant and many community members found the billboards offensive, noting that the company "derives substantial economic benefits" from billboards on Staten Island and asking the company to contact defendant's legal counsel to discuss the matter. The billboard company took the signs down the same day.

The Court of Appeals held that plaintiffs had adequately pled a First Amendment claim; that a jury could find that the defendant's letter contained "an implicit threat of retaliation;" and that a "public-official defendant who threatens to employ coercive state power to stifle protected speech violates a plaintiff's First Amendment rights." …

And the court held that plaintiffs had adequately alleged defamation, despite defendant's claim of absolute privilege:

"… [A]n executive official is absolutely privileged to publish false and defamatory matter of another in the exercise of his executive function if the matter has some relation to the executive proceeding in which the official is acting." … In determining whether absolute privilege applies, the court considers two factors: (1) the personal position or status of the speaker, and (2) the subject matter of the statement and the forum in which it is made in light of the speaker's public duties. Under the second prong, it is not sufficient that the subject matter of defendant's speech merely "relate to" his public duties. Rather, the speech must be made "during his performance of an essential part of his public duties."

Under this authority, defendant is not entitled to dismissal of plaintiffs' defamation claims based on absolute immunity. The general duties of the New York Attorney General are set forth in New York Executive Law § 63. As relevant here, they include: the prosecution and defense of all proceedings in which the state is interested; the investigation, upon the request of the governor or other state officials, of certain indictable offenses; upon the request of the commissioner of labor or the state division of human rights, the prosecution of civil actions for discrimination; the prosecution of criminal offenses; and application to state courts for orders enjoining fraudulent or illegal acts.

In her current papers, defendant also cites N.Y. Exec. Law § 79-n(3), which provides that the attorney general may apply in the name of the state to a court to enjoin unlawful bias-related violence of intimidation. She also cites a penalty provision of an equal rights law that states that notice of any action under that section must be served on the attorney general.

However, the letter to plaintiffs was not written to fulfill any of these duties because defendant had initiated no investigation, prosecution, or any other governmental process against plaintiffs. In fact, defendant does not argue that plaintiffs had engaged in any actual or suspected acts that would fall within the scope of her law-enforcement authority…. Absent some factual predicate for a government official to believe that a citizen may have engaged in conduct that warrants the scrutiny of his or her office, that official is performing no duties that the doctrine of absolute privilege is meant to protect….

Tricia Sophia Lindsay represents plaintiff.

NEXT: Florida Ban on Material Support to "Domestic Terrorist Organizations" Can't Be Applied to Legal Advice to CAIR

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7815. Why Are My Houseplant Leaves Dropping Off in November?

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Houseplants bring so much life and joy to the indoors at this time of the year, so it can be especially distressing to see leaves dropping. The occasional drop of one or two older, spent leaves isn’t a big deal, but if you see green or yellow leaves falling or an excessive leaf drop, you have cause for concern.

Don't panic, though. Fall leaf drop in houseplants doesn’t necessarily mean they’re dying, but it is a sign of distress that you should heed. The transition to fall and winter can be difficult for houseplants, who can struggle to survive changes in lighting, temperature, humidity, and more. Tropical houseplants are particularly susceptible to these shifts. Environmental changes can trigger plants to drop their leaves, and while some simply need an adjustment period to recover, you can speed their journey back to full health by working out what they're particularly unhappy about.

So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Right now, let's identify the kind of leaf drop you’re seeing and the probable cause, and what you should do to set it right. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your houseplant with fallen leaves.

Normal, occasional leaf drop happens when an older leaf, usually near the base of the plant, has yellowed or browned and is ready to drop and make room for new growth. Unusual and more concerning leaf drop shows some characteristic signs:

You might see one or more of these symptoms in your houseplant, and they'll help you identify the cause.

Many of the causes of excessive leaf drop are related to seasonal changes in growing conditions. Observe the symptoms in your plants and the conditions where they’re growing to decide which one, or more than one, of these issues is at play.

While indoor temperature shifts right now might not seem that drastic to you, they can be for houseplants. As the temperatures drop outside, your plants’ locations near windows might be significantly colder than other areas of a room, even with the heat on. They might also be experiencing drafts that were absent in summer and early fall. Colder overall temperatures and changes in temperature throughout the day can both be damaging.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Some signs a plant might be dropping leaves due to temperature shifts include suddenly dropped green leaves, leaves falling after a cold night, or leaf drop on the side of a plant facing a cold draft or window.

Tropical houseplants, and in particular ficus – including fiddle leaf fig, weeping fig and rubber tree plant – are especially sensitive to temperature changes, and are notorious for dropping their leaves after even a subtle shift.

If you’ve had the windows open to enjoy the soft breezes of summer and early fall, closing them up in November can be a shock for houseplants. Turn on the heating, the humidity in the house naturally drops, leaving your plants to grow in dry, stale air.

Low humidity stresses many houseplants and in particular that come from humid tropical or subtropical locations such as Alocasia and Boston ferns. Calathea plants are especially likely to develop dry, crispy leaves that drop. In the dry air, these plants lose more water through their leaves than the roots can replace, and this results in drooping foliage, brown and crispy tips and edges, curling leaves, and increased leaf drop. It’s important to note that dry air can affect plants this way even if the soil is moist.

Late fall and winter bring shorter days and less natural light for plants. This means plants engage in less photosynthesis and grow more slowly, and some go dormant, and leaf drop is a common response. In scientific terms, the lower light conditions accelerate abscission, the natural process that causes plants to shed their leaves.

Stress in the environment can also trigger certain hormones that cause leaves to detach before they’ve reached the end of their natural lifespan. It’s a response that helps a plant reduce the demands of maintaining healthy leaves when conditions aren’t favorable, to help ensure survival. So, while some seasonal leaf drop can be expected at this time of the year, an excessive loss of leaves likely means a stress-related acceleration of the process.

You might be seeing abscission due to lower light levels if plants drop a lot of older, yellow leaves at the base and without other signs of issues, like over- or underwatering. You might also see an overall thinning of the plant and less new growth.

Reduced light levels and slower growth means plants don’t use as much water this time of year, and if you’re watering them like it’s still summer, they're likely overwatered, triggering leaf drop. This is a common reason why houseplants develop yellowing leaves in November. When waterlogged roots start to rot, they can’t absorb nutrients to send to the leaves which consequently turn yellow and drop off. You'll also likely see consistently wet soil, soft stems and mushy roots, and you may notice a sour smell.

Underwatering can be an issue too. If the soil fully dries out for long periods, you might see drooping, curling, or crispy leaves that readily drop off.

Plants that live indoors all year are susceptible to subtle environmental changes in November, but houseplants that spend the summer outside and the winter inside can experience even greater shifts. The change from fresh air, sun, and warmth to drier air and less light indoors is particularly stressful, and they can drop their leaves as a result.

Your plants can also be stressed if you move them to different locations within the home. Fiddle leaf figs are particularly sensitive to being moved once they’re comfortable. Most plants will recover from the shock of moving as long as you provide the right conditions in their new spot.

Environmental stress is the most typical reason for houseplant leaf drop, but be sure to check for pests too. Spider mites are common at this time of the year and an infestation can cause yellowing and leaf drop, especially in warm, dry air when numbers rapidly increase. If you spot fine webbing on the undersides of the leaves and where foliage meets stems, that's a sure sign of spider mites.

Watch out for mealybugs, too, which look like white, cottony lumps often in the joints between leaves and stems. Scale insects appear like small brown bumps on stems and leaves, and can also cause leaves to yellow and drop.

Take action to correct these causes and minimize leaf drop, and houseplants will quickly recover. While some of these steps will be particularly important to put right whatever is the cause of your houseplant's stress, all will help a struggling, stressed plant to recover.

Plants don't respond well to being moved frequently so, rather than continually moving your houseplant around to find a location that suits, do some prep first. A basic thermometer that shows the minimum and maximum temperatures reached like this TempPro Digital Thermometer from Amazon will quickly show you exactly how cozy – or otherwise – a particular spot is. Houseplants prefer stable temperatures and it can be surprising what spikes are caused by heating vents and radiators, and what lows occur near doors, in drafts and on windowsills.

Dry indoor air is a major issue for tropical houseplants native to warm, humid areas. Grouping houseplants together naturally increases humidity around them, and you can easily raise moisture levels further with humidity trays. These are simply shallow trays filled with pebbles that sit beneath the pot, topped up with water that evaporates to increase air humidity. A Bonsai pebble tray such as this from Lowe’s is made for the job, or fashion your own with a plant saucer and pea gravel like this Landscape Rock from The Home Depot.

Another option is to use a humidifier and a portable design like the Homedics Humidifier, available from Amazon, is small enough to sit discreetly in among a group of houseplants.

Instead of relying on guesswork, spend $10 on some simple, no-batteries-required moisture meters like these from Amazon, that tell you when the soil needs some more water. Instead of watering on a set schedule, check the soil on a set schedule instead and you'll naturally adjust irrigation levels in line with houseplants' seasonal needs. Make sure all your plants are in pots with a drainage hole and empty saucers or cachepot after watering to be sure roots aren’t sitting in soggy soil.

If you ever suspect overwatering, always check for root rot by sliding off the pot to check for discolored or mushy stems and a foul smell.

Because of reduced daylight hours and lower position of the sun in the sky through fall and winter, pay extra attention to whether houseplants are getting enough light. East-, west- and south-facing rooms are usually best, and rotate plants to ensure they get light evenly. If there isn't enough natural light in the spot you want to display your plants, use a grow light. These needn't be expensive, as this basic dimmable LED grow light such as this from Walmart proves.

If you see pests or signs of pests, deal with the issue right away and isolate affected plants from others to avoid the infestation spreading. Wipe pests, webbing, honeydew and other residue from leaves with a soft cloth, and remove any foliage that is very badly damaged. Finally, if necessary, use an insecticidal soap or neem oil like Captain Jack's Neem Oil Spray, available from Amazon, to manage a pest infestation.

Some plants like caladiums and elephant ear go dormant this time of year, so losing leaves in November is a natural and normal part of their lifecycle. As they're not actively growing, they're better placed in a cooler but not cold part of the house and watering significantly reduced.

The right cordless screwdriver depends on the job. Compact models suit light household tasks, while more powerful ones handle dense wood.

For instance, a compact inline driver may be easier to maneuver inside furniture, while a pistol-grip model can provide more power. To earn a spot in our lineup, a cordless screwdriver had to be easy to use, durable, and capable of everyday fastening tasks, with a battery that lasted through small projects. The screwdriver generates up to 1,300 RPM at top speed, which is quite an accomplishment for an automatic screwdriver.

It also packs some powerful torque, which meant we were able to insert screws with ease into drywall, pine, and birch boards. With that much torque, the 21-adjustment clutch is essential to prevent stripping out the screw heads.

Still, it’s so good at sensing circuits that you could reserve this cordless screwdriver solely for electrical maintenance jobs.

Get the Skil cordless screwdriver at Amazon, Menards, or Acme Tools.

The Amazon Basics (formerly Denali) screwdriver doesn’t boast many bells and whistles, but it lets you choose from three torque settings. We found that handy when inserting screws into materials with different densities—for instance, more torque when inserting screws in wood than in softer drywall. It also features an LED guide light, but we found it to be dim and unlikely to offer much illumination in low-light situations.

The screwdriver charges via a USB-C cord (included). We liked this setup, as it simplifies charging—no need to remove and charge the battery separately. A compact tool measuring about 7 inches long, it was useful in restricted spots, but we would have liked a convertible grip. A barrel grip is excellent in some situations, but a convertible pistol grip would add versatility.

The only real downside we noted was that this model tended to bog down a little when we inserted screws in wood. It did the job, but it took longer than it did on drywall. Still, this is a handy little cordless screwdriver to have around the house or to keep in the trunk of a car for when small jobs arise.

Get the Amazon Basics cordless screwdriver at Amazon.

We tested 12 cordless screwdrivers from 10 brands, considering price, battery design, included accessories, grip, speed, torque control, and features such as work lights and interchangeable heads. We drove dozens of fasteners with each tool, using prefab holes, predrilled holes, and raw wood; earlier tests also included drywall, pine, and birch.

We noted how comfortably each screwdriver fit in the hand, how easily we could change bits and direction, and whether the screwdriver had enough power to seat screws without damaging their heads. After testing, we rated each model on a five-point scale for ease of use, build quality, performance, and value, using those scores and our hands-on notes to select the picks in this guide.

A slim cordless screwdriver can reach spots a drill can’t as easily. A cordless screwdriver drives screws faster than a manual screwdriver and reduces wrist strain by eliminating the need for repeated wrist motions. Its light weight and battery power also make it easy to carry from one task to the next. As you shop, consider where you’ll use it and how much power and control your projects require.

The more power a cordless screwdriver has, the faster it can turn. While cordless screwdrivers don’t require the amount of power that a drill driver or an impact driver might have, they still need enough juice to get the job done. If you’re purchasing a straight barrel-type driver, consider one with a speed between 300 and 500 RPM. This range is ideal for loosening or tightening a screw quickly without being too fast to handle. With pistol-grip models, speeds above 1,000 RPM are easier to control.

The more torque your screwdriver has, the denser the material that it can drive a fastener into. Heavy-duty screwdrivers provide more torque and may be suitable for driving a few drywall screws into wood studs, but this can drain the battery quickly.

Small cordless screwdrivers can reach and manipulate various types of screws into awkward spaces much more easily than a manual tool can. As long as there’s room for the tip of the driver to fit onto the fastener, you’re set—a powered screwdriver will help do the rest.

To fit into such tight places, the best cordless screwdrivers are highly maneuverable. A slim, compact design helps, and many models also have rotating handles that swap from a straight grip to a pistol grip, like those seen on drills and screw guns. Also, a smaller battery size makes cordless screwdrivers easier to tuck between boards and other low-clearance scenarios, such as behind sinks for plumbing tasks.

Many cordless screwdrivers come with rechargeable batteries, and they tend to range between 4 and 8 volts. Since a cordless screwdriver requires much less speed and power than a drill, these lower voltages are adequate. Two benefits of a smaller, lower-voltage battery? It fits in smaller places than full-size options, and it helps make the rechargeable screwdriver as light as possible.

Some lower-end screwdrivers use replaceable batteries. These models are less convenient and more expensive, since you have to replace batteries frequently. They usually have less power and torque as well.

If you have a large project coming up, it helps if a cordless screwdriver has enough power to see it through to the end. Luckily, battery life isn’t much of a concern for most of the best cordless screwdrivers because their small motors don’t use as much battery energy as a large motor does.

However, some cordless screwdrivers have a battery-level indicator that alerts users when the battery is running low. It’s helpful to know the battery status so that you can juice it up while on a lunch or supply-run break. Many models take about an hour to recharge.

Cordless screwdrivers tighten or loosen screws in prethreaded holes. They’re perfect for screws in electrical boxes and fixtures, screws used in automotive interiors and appliances, installing door locks and cabinet hardware, and other mechanical settings with threaded holes.

Except for the most heavy-duty electrical screwdrivers, these tools aren’t typically designed for lag screws and bolts, wood screws, or fasteners in other dense materials. While it’s technically possible to drive a screw through drywall with one of these tools, that’s simply not the type of job they’re made for. For this situation, grab a drill or an impact driver instead.

Cordless screwdrivers use toolless chucks, so swapping between bits is quick and easy. These chucks fit ¼-inch bits—the same bits used in standard multi-bit manual screwdrivers. There are also ¼-inch-drive drill bits, allowing a screwdriver to be used as a drill in light-duty material like thin wood or plastics.

The variety of ¼-inch bits available makes cordless screwdrivers incredibly useful: For instance, you can alternate from driving Phillips head screws to removing Allen or Torx screws in seconds. Most cordless screwdrivers use magnets to hold the bits in place while also providing a bit of magnetism to keep the screw on the end of the bit.

The clutch in fastening tools regulates the amount of torque applied to a fastener. Once the set torque is reached, the clutch will start to “slip,” preventing the tool from driving the fastener or drilling any deeper. Simply adjust the clutch according to the fastener and material type. Since this is situation-specific, the rule of thumb is to set the clutch to a low setting and increase slowly as needed.

Too much torque can break smaller, older, or low-quality fasteners. Fortunately, the best cordless screwdrivers have adjustable clutch settings to avoid stripping or breaking these fasteners. The clutch can also avoid overdriving the screw too deeply, which may also cause unwanted results.

Torque settings can make a significant difference when working with old, stubborn fasteners. Instead of tearing the heads off screws or stripping the fastener beyond recognition, the clutch will begin to slip, preventing the driver from continuing to turn and causing damage.

Not all cordless screwdrivers have adjustable clutches, though. Some don’t have the power to require one. However, higher-end screwdrivers with more torque usually do.

By the time a project with a lot of assembly is finished, your forearm and hand might be tired from using a manual screwdriver. Lesson learned: To forgo hand and arm fatigue, opt for a cordless screwdriver. This’ll also save you energy and time, allowing you to move on to the next project faster.

Being able to see what you’re doing is key to a quality finished project. If, while using a drill, the tool keeps getting in the way, it may slip off the screw, marring the surface or scratching the workpiece. Cordless screwdrivers let users see what they’re doing since a hand won’t block the view.

Instead of carrying several screwdrivers around in a tool box or tool belt, it can be easier to tote just one cordless model. Since the bits are easy to swap, a complete bit set can reduce the overall weight and free up space in a belt for other tools. It’s much easier to carry one cordless screwdriver with eight tips than eight separate screwdrivers.

A cordless screwdriver is a tool that many reach for again and again for a host of different tasks. Here are a few ways to get the most help from this handy tool.

There’s a lot to consider when choosing a new cordless screwdriver, so you may still have questions. If you’re still wondering about the ins and outs of cordless screwdrivers, check out these answers to some commonly asked questions.

A cordless screwdriver is a battery-powered tool that tightens and loosens screws with a motor and trigger rather than relying on hand power.

Cordless drills for DIYers accept several drill bit sizes with adjustable chucks, while mini cordless screwdrivers only accept ¼-inch bits. Also, cordless drills tend to be more adjustable in terms of speed, letting the user drill into different materials accurately and efficiently.

There are a few slightly different methods for operating a cordless screwdriver, but here is a general usage guideline:1. Choose the right bit and place it in the chuck.2. Adjust the direction you want to drive the screw (tighten or loosen) with the switch on the screwdriver.3. Seat the bit completely into the head of the screw.4. Maintain pressure on the fastener and squeeze the trigger.

Yes, higher voltage tends to be better for cordless tools, but there are some caveats. Cordless tools with higher voltages are certainly more powerful, but that power comes at a cost. They weigh more and are less compact than lower-voltage options. For cordless screwdrivers, 4 to 8 volts is usually sufficient, especially for light-duty tasks.

Yes, but it depends on how often you’ll use them and the tasks you do most often. They can save quite a bit of time and effort and can increase your efficiency, all at a typically affordable price.

#7812. "Emphatic Swearing"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I was just listening to a great talk about taboo words by Steven Pinker at the FIRE Soapbox conference, and particularly liked this example of "emphatic swearing":

The taboo word is often used to draw a listener's attention, emphasizing the following noun or adjective. For example: "This is really, really fucking brilliant" [that's a reference to the Bono incident that led to FCC action -EV] or "He thinks he's a fucking scoutmaster, Rip Van fuckin' Winkle."

When emphatic and idiomatic swearing is overused, it can lead to a form of English sometimes referred to as "fuck patois." This is a style where swearing is so pervasive that it becomes almost a defining feature of the language. An example of this can be found in the story of a soldier who says, "I come home to my fucking house after three fucking years in the fucking war, and what do I fucking well find? My wife in bed, engaged in illicit sexual relations with a male!"

I think there's more going on in the soldier story than just fuck patois—indeed, what makes it emphatic might be the absence of "fuck" in the closing phrase—but in any event it's pretty funny.

Note that the term "fuck patois" is often credited to Tom Wolfe.

#7811. Kathy’s Fall Garden

Happy Monday, GPOD! Halloween may be behind us, but fall still has plenty to offer in Kathy’s Zone 6a garden. I love how she keeps the seasonal decorating simple and lets what’s already happening in the landscape do most of the work. A few pumpkins, a refreshed container, and plants still hanging onto their color are enough to make the whole front garden feel ready for November.

Keeping it sweet and simple this fall! It has been a beautiful fall in Michigan so far. Although I’ve been gardening for more than 40 years, this is my eighth year gardening at our current home in Macomb.

I love these Japanese forest grasses (Hakonechloa macra cvs., Zones 5–9).

I replaced this summer container display earlier than usual, and these plants have been hanging tough since the first week of September.

Just sweet! There has been a multitude of fancy pumpkins for sale this year, more than usual, and I think they are so pretty!

Boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), Fire Chief arborvitae (Thuja occidentalis ‘Congabe’, Zones 5–8), ‘Orange Rocket’ Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii ‘Orange Rocket’, Zones 4–9), and Little Lime® panicle hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata ‘Jane’, Zones 3–8) grow in front of our home.

Already, I’m looking forward to spring when I can plant this new garden arch! I’m thinking clematis (Clematis cvs., Zones 3–9).

Here is Belleza Dark Pink gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri ‘KLEAU04263’, Zones 6–9) and yellow ‘Lady Stratheden’ avens (Geum ‘Lady Stratheden’, Zones 5–9). They are hanging tough so far!

Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Kathy! I really like the little bed by the driveway. The purple tones of the ajuga carpeting the ground against that bright orange mum and the pumpkins make for such an effortlessly beautiful fall display. And I’m with you on already thinking about spring—I’d love to see what you decide to grow over that new arch!

#7810. Arkansas Constitution's Right to Bear Arms Provision Strengthened

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The old provision dated back to 1868, and read, "The citizens of this State shall have the right to keep and bear arms, for their common defense." The new, which passed 71%-29%, will read:

(a) The citizens of this State shall have the right to keep and bear arms, for: (1) Their common defense; (2) Lawful hunting and recreational use; and (3) Any other lawful purpose. (b) The right to keep and bear arms under subsection (a) of this section includes without limitation the possession and use of: (1) Ammunition; (2) Firearm accessories; and (3) Firearm components. (c) The right to keep and bear arms under subsection (a) of this section is a natural, fundamental, and individual right that shall not be infringed.

#7809. What Does a Green Porch Light Mean? The Tradition, Explained

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Savannah Sher, Updated by Daryna Tobey

Published Nov 5, 2026 12:01 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

In November, you may notice your neighbors replacing their white porch light bulbs with green bulbs. While it’s easy to assume that they’re getting a head start on their Christmas decorating, green porch lights have a significance that has nothing to do with the holiday season. Americans use green porch lights to show support for U.S. military veterans. The idea began as part of the “Greenlight a Vet” project. According to the campaign, “The simple action of changing one light to green is intended to spark a national conversation regarding the recognition of veterans, and ‘greenlight’ them forward as valued members of our communities.”

In 2013, Walmart’s Veterans Welcome Home Commitment initiative, which provides jobs to any honorably discharged U.S. veteran, created an ad campaign asking people to turn on a green porch light as a way to recognize and show appreciation for veterans in their community. They encouraged people to share their support on social media by taking a photo of their green light and sharing it with the hashtag #GreenlightAVet.

The Greenlight a Vet initiative is not the only one to shine a light, so to speak, on our country’s veterans. In 2022, The National Association of Counties (NACo) in affiliation with the National Association of County Veterans Services Officers (NACVSO), launched Operation Green Light for Veterans (#OperationGreenLight). In the program’s debut year, over 300 counties participated nationwide, including Fairbanks, Alaska’s North Star Borough and Mohave County, Arizona. Nicole Weissman, NACo’s director of strategic communications, expects the number of participating counties this year to be “significantly larger” than it was last year.

“We must support our veterans and their families—not only during Operation Green Light but all year round,” says NACo President Jo McGuire. “Counties are advocating for legislation to secure appropriate resources at the local level to help veterans access their federal benefits, ease their transition into civilian life, and support their long-term health and well-being.”

The association explains, “By shining a green light, county governments and our residents will let veterans know that they are seen, appreciated, and supported.” NACo’s initiative encourages all U.S. counties and parishes to show support for military veterans by illuminating courthouses, offices, and other municipal buildings in green from November 4 to 11, the week leading up to Veterans Day.

In September 2023, the House of Representatives introduced House Resolution 750, a bipartisan bill recognizing Operation Green Light for Veterans for “supporting veterans and…help[ing] veterans transition to civilian life.”

Illuminate Enbrighten’s waterproof Eternity lights green for Veterans Day and leave them up year round, changing colors and modes via app.

Green is a color that is often associated with the military because of the green uniforms traditionally worn by troops, but there’s a more symbolic meaning as well. According to the Greenlight a Vet campaign, “Green is the color of hope, renewal and well-being.” They add that “‘Greenlight’ is also a term commonly used to activate forward movement.”

Govee’s smart light bulbs support millions of hues and can be controlled by phone app. Read the review.

While Veterans Day on November 11 is the most symbolic time of year to show support for America’s troops, why not follow Operation Green Light for Veterans’ lead and shine the light for the whole week of Veterans Day, or even keep your green light up year-round to show your ongoing appreciation for our military?

In Prattville, Alabama, community advocate Julie Cooley, who is also a military spouse and mother, went a little further. She encouraged “neighbors, municipalities and businesses to show their love and support of our veterans this week. Some choose to put signage on their marquis, some offer discounts, some turn their lights green! What’s important is that our military veterans and their families feel a great big hug from their Prattville community.”

“One of NACo’s goals for Operation Green Light is to equip counties to participate in a way that’s meaningful to veterans in their community, so we’re always looking for ways to do that,” says Weissman. In some counties, she says, this outreach includes “distributing green light bulbs or otherwise encouraging residents to participate” in Operation Green Light for Veterans.  If you’d like to show your support for veterans this month, pick up a green light bulb at your local hardware store—or at one of the following retailers.

#7808. 6 Ways to Stop Chimney Fires Before They Start

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 5, 2026 12:46 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

There are more than 25,000 chimney fires incurring $125 million-plus in property damage every year in the United States. That damage is largely due to flames in the lower chimney migrating upward to crack, warp, melt, or otherwise negatively affect the masonry or metal chimney walls. In the most severe cases, chimney fires can destroy houses and put lives at risk. These tragedies are often preventable: Failure to regularly inspect, repair, and clean a chimney can cause it to malfunction or collect dangerous buildup that puts your family at risk.

If you practice these prevention tips, that hard-working column above your fireplace or wood stove should continue to do its job of ushering smoke and other by-products out of your home, so you and yours can safely cozy up in front of the flames. Ahead, learn what causes chimney fires and steps you can take to prevent them.

The main culprit of chimney fires is creosote. This highly flammable, dark brown substance coats chimney walls when by-products of a fire (smoke, vapor, and unburned wood) condense as they move from the hot fireplace or wood stove into the cooler chimney. If the temperature in the chimney flue (the space inside the chimney) is high enough, and the creosote build-up thick enough, creosote can catch fire—and that fire can spread and move up the flue.

To minimize creosote build-up, only burn seasoned hardwood that has dried for at least six months and contains a moisture content of no more than 20 percent, which you can easily test with a wood moisture meter. And remember to always keep the damper (a metal plate in the flue that regulates the draft) open during a fire to maintain adequate airflow.

And if your chimney’s flue liner (the layer between the flue and chimney walls) is uninsulated, it’s recommended to insulate it by either wrapping a heat-resistant insulation blanket around the liner or pouring an insulation mix like vermiculite into the space between the flue liner and flue. An insulated flue liner will prevent flue temperatures from getting too cool—a condition that could encourage fire by-products to condense and form creosote.

Because many defects that lead to chimney fires, such as a cracked flue liner, aren’t visible to the naked eye, it’s crucial to have a Chimney Safety Institute of America-certified chimney sweep inspect your fireplace or woodstove, chimney, and venting system once a year. This pro will inform you of any damage and, if desired, repair it as well as remove soot, creosote, or obstructions such as bird nests.

There are three levels of chimney inspections:

Consult your chimney sweep company about which inspection level is recommended for your chimney and venting system.

If when you scratch a finger against a chimney wall and uncover one-eighth of an inch of build-up, it’s time for a cleaning. A professional chimney cleaning costs between $100 and $350 and usually includes a sweep of the outside of the chimney along with the firebox, the smoke shelf, the smoke chamber above the firebox, the flue, and the flue liner. However, budget-conscious DIYers willing to get up on a ladder can also clean their chimney without professional help by using a wide chimney brush.

This creosote destroyer coats your chimney liner with protective chemicals while you burn, preventing creosote buildup. Read our full review.

Leaves and animal nests inside a flue can quickly fuel a chimney fire when touched by loose embers from a fire. A chimney cap on the crown around the outside opening of the flue will keep debris and critters out. The cap will also prevent “back puffing,” whereby escaped smoke from a fire re-enters the chimney and then the home. Caps also prevent acidic rainwater from entering and corroding the chimney. Expect to spend anywhere from $50 for galvanized metal caps to $500 or more for decorative models. While some homeowners opt to put in a chimney cap themselves, self-installation may void the warranty—it may be worth it to call a pro.

Always stick to the best fire starters when selecting fuel, kindling, and tinder.

Low-temperature, slow-burning fires, particularly those left to smolder overnight, produce more smoke and leave behind more unburned combustible material. When that hardens into creosote on the chimney walls, there’s an increased risk of chimney fires. Hot, fast-burning fires, on the other hand, leave far less smoke, vapor, and unburned wood behind, so little to no creosote forms.

The best way to burn a clean fire is to use the top-down burn method: Place the large logs vertically at the bottom of the fireplace or wood stove (with the bottoms of the logs facing you), add four to five horizontal layers of kindling, then top with tinder and light.

And, before retiring for the night, always extinguish the fire: Spread out the wood and embers with a fireplace poker, then cover them with the ash lying at the bottom of the fireplace using a fireplace shovel. Then douse the cooled wood and embers with enough baking soda to cover them completely—the sodium bicarbonate will extinguish any remaining embers. After the firebox cools (for a minimum of three hours, but preferably eight), shovel the ashes into a metal container. Fill the metal container with water and store it outside the home away from other flammable materials until you’re ready to discard them.

#7807. A November Garden Walk in Downtown Milwaukee

November is definitely settling in here in downtown Milwaukee, Wisconsin (Zone 6a). Most of the summer flowers are gone, leaves are piling up, and plenty of perennials are heading into dormancy. But there’s still so much to appreciate. Today we’re staying close to home for a walk around my neighborhood. I walk these streets with my dog all the time, and there are a handful of gardens I always slow down to admire.

Starting off strong with this one! This prairie-inspired garden is always buzzing with pollinators in summer, and it’s one of my favorites to walk by. In fall, the large sweeps of switchgrass (Panicum virgatum, Zones 4–9) and little bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium, Zones 3–9) really come forward. And wow, those fluffy switchgrass plumes make a statement when planted en masse.

From the other side, the pinkish-copper tones of little bluestem become much more prominent. The planting even carries across the sidewalk into the curb strip, making this small garden pretty hard to miss.

A few houses down is another garden that inspires me. The whole yard is planted so elegantly, with interest no matter the season. Bare spaces are usually filled with annuals. But even in November, we still get to see roses in bloom and hydrangeas giving it their all to remain relevant. The urn in the background with the pumpkin is a lovely seasonal touch.

This garden might look messy to some, but this is the kind of fall mess I truly enjoy. The hostas (Hosta cvs., Zones 3–9) spilling over the stairs, surrounded and covered by fallen red maple leaves… I love it!

This deep burgundy shrub covered in bright red berries certainly caught my eye. Unfortunately, it’s Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii, Zones 4–8), an invasive shrub here in Wisconsin. If you like the look, consider one of these native alternatives to Japanese barberry, including chokeberry, fothergilla, Virginia sweetspire, summersweet, and inkberry.

This Siberian crab apple (Malus baccata, Zones 2–7) is absolutely covered in clusters of warm orange fruit. Once so many summer flowers have disappeared, fruiting trees like this become some of the strongest color in the landscape.

It’s nice to see another garden extend beyond the front yard and into the curb strip. These often-overlooked spaces have so much potential. They can become a small garden, pollinator planting, or even a bee lawn.

And, of course, who can resist a strip of marigolds (Tagetes cvs., annual)? Especially when they’re still looking this good!

And one final reminder to leave the leaves this fall! Fallen leaves provide important overwintering habitat for pollinators and other beneficial insects, so leaving some in garden beds gives them a place to shelter until spring.

Thanks for coming along on my afternoon walk! While I wish this were a fall update from my little concrete jungle of a backyard, it’s all packed up now… because I’m moving to Georgia in just a few short weeks! I’ll definitely miss these neighborhood gardens, but I’m excited to see what new gardens and plants catch my eye down South.

Have photos to share? We’d love to see your garden, a particular collection of plants you love, or a wonderful garden you had the chance to visit!
