#7806. 2027 Garden Planning: What the Experts Say Will Be Big Next Year

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 5, 2026 4:51 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

There’s always something new and exciting on the horizon in the world of gardening. Around this time every year, various organizations release their favorite gardening and landscaping trends for the coming year. From the color of the year to new plants and outdoor décor, the list below represents our favorite 2027 gardening trends for you to consider as you plan or update your outdoor space in the coming months.

Garden Media Group has identified ancient blue as the garden color of the year for 2027. As the first manufactured color in history, blue was created by the Egyptians 5,000 years ago to imitate precious lapis lazuli. While blue is consistently the favorite color around the world, it is the rarest color in the garden, showing up in fewer than 10 percent of flowers. “This makes growing it in the garden feel like victory,” says Katie Dubow, president of Garden Media Group.

Here are some planting and décor tips to seamlessly incorporate this calming color into your garden:

Gardeners prefer more from their edible plants than just fruits and vegetables to harvest, according to Monrovia’s 2027 Garden Design Trends Study. “We’re seeing shoppers be more discerning in their edible choices,” says Katie Tamony, chief marketing officer and trend spotter at Monrovia. “They’re looking for plants that add a design element or feel more exotic than the common choices their neighbors grow. People are also interested in edible plants that look good all season long.”

Adding an edible garden ranks among the highest-interest projects in Monrovia’s survey, with more than 45 percent of respondents saying they are looking for more unique selections. Enhance your edible garden with specialty herbs; berries with year-round interest; and conversation-starting selections like pomegranate, figs, kiwi, and olives.

After years of beige minimalism and tidy rows of shrubs, the “Let’s Go Rococo” theme is all about exuberance over restraint, says Dubow. Emerging in early 18th century France, rococo design was a deliberate rebellion by artists and craftsmen against the stiff grandeur of Baroque and societal wealth inequality. Think flowers, shells, gilded flourishes, ruffles, jewel-tone palettes, and asymmetry. “It’s ornamental, romantic, a little over the top, and joyful,” notes Dubow.

Here are some ways to infuse rococo style into your garden:

Garden Media Group’s OutdooRx trend positions the garden as medicine, says Dubow. “In the United Kingdom, doctors now “socially prescribe” gardening programs to patients, and research continues to show that gardening lowers stress hormones like cortisol while boosting mood-lifting dopamine and serotonin,” she explains. Approaches like the Sunday Garden Trend can provide relaxation.

Fortunately, you don’t need a prescription to benefit. You can create a therapeutic garden in your own backyard with these helpful tips:

This long-handle digging tool allows gardeners to work the soil more comfortably (and for longer periods of time) from a standing position.

National Garden Bureau also tracks garden trends, especially when it comes to which specific plants are the most popular in a given year. “Coming up in 2027, we see an enormous interest in hellebores, and that is our Year of the Crop for Perennials,” says Diane Blazek, executive director for All-America Selections at National Garden Bureau.

Often called the Christmas rose or Lenten rose, the hellebore is a hardy perennial that does well in full shade and brings beauty to winter and early spring gardens when most other flowers have faded. It produces elegant 2- to 3-inch blossoms in a cup shape that resemble roses. Hellebore flowers grow in a variety of colors, so you have plenty of options. It grows in USDA Hardiness Zones 5 to 8, and does best in cottage gardens, winter gardens, or woodland gardens. Take note that this plant is toxic and should be handled with caution.

As another season of the popular show The Gilded Age is released this month, romance and beauty are alive and well in gardens, too. This look maximizes the popularity of European-inspired garden design with an elevated, modern twist, shining a spotlight on classic plants like roses, peonies, hydrangeas, and boxwood. In addition to these timeless plants, this trend showcases artful hedges, chartreuse foliage, and collector statement plants.

“This trend appeals to established gardeners,” says Tamony. “Homeowners who have invested in their interior design are taking that high-end look to the garden.” Their interest in rare, collector plants is increasing, and Monrovia’s research shows their willingness to pay for premium plants and exquisite blooms is up between 5 and 9 percent since 2025.

Another style that is expected to be popular is the Palm Springs outdoor space. This works well for gardeners looking to create an attractive desert oasis through containers as well as the landscape. “The Palm Springs Style trend is all about creating a calming, wellness-focused outdoor space that feels more upscale,” says Tamony. With this aesthetic, gardeners can transform their landscape by choosing structured succulents and lush, tropical colors found with species from Agave, Bougainvillea, Mandevilla, and tropical hibiscus.

We’ll help you set up your first garden—whether that’s a few pots on your patio, a raised bed, or an in-ground plot out back—and select the right plants for your soil and region.

#7805. Short Circuit: A roundup of recent federal court decisions

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Geek therapy, crack felony, and some Scooby Snacks.

Please enjoy the latest edition of Short Circuit, a weekly feature written by a bunch of people at the Institute for Justice.

New on the Short Circuit podcast: We look at 100 years of zoning and chances of zoning reform, in court and in city councils, with Harvard's Molly Brady and Vice Mayor of Cambridge, Mass., Burhan Azeem.

And on the latest episode of the Law Office History podcast, Christian Burset of Penn Law explains how it was hard to be a textualist in Olde Timey England because Parliament wasn't very clear when writing its statutes and it was hard to find copies of them anyway.

Protectionism alert! This week, IJ sent a letter to officials in Clewiston, Florida, warning that the city's food truck ordinance violates the Florida Constitution. Food trucks in Clewiston may only operate on Mondays and Tuesdays and must stay at least 200 feet away from any open restaurant unless that restaurant gives written permission. Those two days are not a coincidence. Mondays and Tuesdays are when most brick-and-mortar restaurants in Clewiston are closed, meaning the ordinance permits food trucks only when they are unlikely to compete with established businesses. The 200-foot buffer zone fulfills a similar protectionist function, giving existing restaurants veto power over whether a competitor can set up nearby.

NEXT: Arkansas Constitution's Right to Bear Arms Provision Strengthened

John Ross is the editor of the Short Circuit newsletter and the producer of the Bound By Oath podcast, two incomparable projects of surpassing importance from the Institute for Justice.

Whether it’s for security or style, investing in solar gutter lights is an affordable way to upgrade any home. Though they aren’t quite as easy to install as solar lanterns, most solar gutter lights are generally easy to put up, typically attaching via clips to a home’s gutters. They can be installed as temporary or permanent fixtures that convert the day’s sun into attractive lighting on the exterior of a home. Many lights also include additional mounting hardware so they can be used above doorways, along fence posts, and as deck lights, making them both solar security lights and architectural features on a home’s exterior.

We recently hands-on tested five sets of solar gutter lights against 2 weeks of wind, rain, and plenty of sunshine to see how they held up. Though there were a number of winners, the UniqueFire Outdoor Solar Gutter Lights are our favorites. We like them for their durable construction, attractive design, and affordable price point.

While the price of solar gutter lights can be a factor, appearance and durability take center stage. Since they’ll be placed on the exterior of the home, it’s important to choose a style that matches a home’s aesthetic. And because these lights are frequently installed at high points on a home, low maintenance is key; no one wants to climb on a roof or up a ladder if they don’t have to. We took all this into account during our tests, and the result is the following list of the best solar gutter lights for the job.

Bottom line: Solar gutter lights offer an easy, cost-effective way to enhance home security and style. UniqueFire stands out as the best overall choice.

The following products are some of the best solar gutter lights on the market, including the five we tested for durability, light quality, installation, and water resistance. We’ve highlighted our favorite features below and included three additional picks we think are worth checking out for shoppers looking for the best solar gutter lights.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Appearance 5/5; Light Quality 5/5; Durability 5/5; Value 5/5

With its easy-to-install bracket system, this set of six solar gutter lights was up on our house in just minutes. Once the lights were installed, we noticed that the added design element gave them an upgraded feel, despite their affordability. Because the lights can be purchased in either black or white, they can blend in with a wide range of home styles (although some buyers may prefer a rounded or smaller light). The lights come on automatically once it’s dark out and shut off before sunrise.

The lights themselves give off plenty of light, and we found the rectangle style to be more appealing if used on a fence post or railing. The solar-powered gutter lights stood up well to the elements and kept on shining throughout our test period. Because the manufacturer recommends replacing the rechargeable AA battery after 8 to 12 months, this may be an important detail for some buyers to factor in.

What our tester says: “Overall, we found these lights easy to put up, attractive, and at such a great price that we gave them the top spot on our list.”—Amber Guetebier, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the UniqueFire solar gutter lights at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Appearance 4/5; Light Quality 4.5/5; Durability 4/5; Value 5/5

Falove’s outdoor solar gutter lights are available in a pack of eight, allowing users to set up an entire light scheme with one kit at a very reasonable price. They take just a few minutes to set up, but there’s one small issue: One of the included screws is a very small thumb screw and requires an equally small screwdriver to put in place. We ended up using an eyeglass kit to tighten it. While the process was straightforward, it was a little tedious, and installing several of these could get old fast.

Some LED gutter lights can seem too bright in a garden or backyard setting, but each of these lights is just 100 lumens, which illuminated the space nicely and gave the house an atmospheric glow. This set has a simple appearance, but it will blend in with most home styles. The bracket has two mounting options: one with the tiny screw that can be easily clipped onto the gutter lip, or a more permanent mounting onto a fence or other structure (this method comes with a much longer standard-size screw). Overall, these are pleasing lights, and they come at a very affordable price point. Like others, they came on once it was dark and turned off before sunrise.

Get the Falove solar gutter lights at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Setup 4.5/5; Appearance 4/5; Light Quality 5/5; Durability 5/5; Value 4.5/5

The InnoGear solar gutter lights come in a pack of two. Since each light produces 450 lumens, these are bright lights worth checking out. The lights feature several modes, including low output, medium output, motion sensor, and full brightness, with a few combinations of these as well. For example, you can keep it on low mode combined with motion detection, and the light automatically brightens to full mode when it detects movement. For this reason, these are an excellent option for solar-powered security lights. They switch on automatically once it’s dark and switch back off at dawn.

The lights mount directly to the structure of a home. However, although these are advertised as solar gutter lights, they are not able to clip directly onto gutters like most gutter lights. They can be mounted either flush against the home like a sconce or with the included bar, which allows for positioning beyond eaves to ensure maximum light absorption. Because they look a little like miniature solar panels, they have a modern feel that may not appeal to everyone’s sense of style. Overall, these are high-quality outdoor solar security lights that passed all of the environmental tests with flying colors.

For some high-powered accent lighting around the home, shoppers can check out the DBF solar gutter lights. The lights in this six-pack use a two-way bracket that can clamp to gutters with the included thumb screw or screw directly into the structure of a fence or home. Each light produces up to 100 lumens and can run for more than 10 hours, coming on when it gets dark and shutting off closer to sunrise. We tested the black color with cool white light, but they are also available in white and with a warm white light.

These lights received high marks for ease of installation after we were able to decipher the cryptic directions. Because they are similar to other solar gutter lights that clamp in place, we were able to install them without too much trouble. However, someone who has no experience with these kinds of lights may find themselves looking up video tutorials. Though these are a little pricier than we think they ought to be, they are frequently marked down on Amazon, making them a better buy for the money than they may seem at first glance. Their unique UFO-like shape puts off a vaguely midcentury modern vibe, which may be appealing to some shoppers.

The following solar gutter lights all received high marks from online reviews or are additional solar lights for gutters from brands we’ve reviewed. Though we did not personally put each product to the test as with the previous five, they’re worth checking out based on factors like price, style, design, and collective reviews.

Not all landscapes call for bright, glaring lights. For those who want something more subtle, iSunMoon’s six-pack of solar gutter lights might be a great inexpensive lighting idea for the yard. While most reviewers agree this is not enough light to really illuminate a walkway, it provides a glowing light that creates a nice ambience.

These lights get high marks for easy installation, and after installing five different types of solar gutter lights, we can tell from the images they are nearly identical in installation to others on this list. However, they are definitely less bright, and we can’t swear by their weather resistance, especially because no IP rating is provided, which indicates how well an electrical product stands up to water and dust.

Get the iSunMoon solar gutter lights at Amazon.

Creative Design’s solar gutter lights offer a blend of bright light and flexibility. This two-pack of lights produces 500 lumens per light of brightness. They also have adjustable modes, givingusers a choice between low, medium, and high outputs, as well as motion sensing.

The manufacturer states these lights can stay lit for up to 12 hours. They come with all the hardware required to attach them directly to the gutters and brackets to hold them out from under the eaves for optimal sunlight.

Get the Creative Design solar gutter lights at Amazon.

When we tested InnoGear’s 80 LED solar lights, we gave them high marks for durability, versatility, and brightness. For this reason, we feel that this set of four InnoGear 24 LED solar lights is worth checking out. Each light produces 150 lumens and stays in dim mode until motion is detected within a 10- to 20-foot range. Once motion stops, the lights go back to dim but remain on.

These lights are an inexpensive way to create more security for a home. However, buyers will want to be aware that these do not clip onto gutters, nor do they have an additional bar for extended installation. These models are sconce-style only. Similar to the other InnoGear lights on this list, they have the appearance of small solar panels.

Get the InnoGear motion sensor solar gutter lights at Amazon.

To test the best solar gutter lights, we installed each light and took note of how easy or difficult the assembly and installation process was. We recorded the charging time for each and whether the lights performed well on sunny days, cloudy days and after a rainstorm. We noted how bright the lights were and if there were any additional features, such as motion detection or the ability to pivot or adjust the lights. The lights were left up for 2 weeks, including during a heavy summer rainstorm.

Each tested solar gutter light was evaluated on a scale of 1 to 5 across multiple categories: setup, appearance, light quality, durability, and value. We compiled the totals to get the rating for each category and ranked the solar gutter lights accordingly.

Before shopping for the best solar lights, there are some points to consider. Below are some of the factors that go into choosing the best solar gutter lights to help you decide which type is best for your specific application.

Note: These kinds of lights run independently of solar roof lights, a solar power system, or solar generator, so they don’t require any hardwiring or complicated installation.

Similar to solar garden path lights, the best solar gutter lights come in a wide range of brightness levels. Your lighting needs will determine which product is best for you. Many small clip-on lights offer just enough accent lighting to add a tasteful glow to your property. These lights provide between 20 and 50 lumens each, which is enough to illuminate a garden bed or a bit of a walkway relatively well.

For more light, there are models available with outputs over 500 lumens. These lights are excellent for lighting a driveway, fence line, or other areas you’d prefer to keep brightly lit.

Since most solar gutter lights attach directly to a home’s gutters, the materials chosen are an important factor. A light made with bulky materials, such as heavy-duty metal, will eventually bend and deform a gutter, so heft is worth considering.

By and large, the best solar gutter lights are made of plastic. These lights are lightweight but durable enough to withstand the elements. However, the brackets used to clip them to the gutter are usually steel, which gives these units the strength they need to withstand wind and heavy rains. Some of the lights that attach directly to the home’s structure might be aluminum, which is a more corrosion-resistant material than steel, and it’s also lighter weight.

Another important consideration is the IP rating. An IP rating (or Ingress Protection rating) indicates how well a light can stand up to elements like dust and water. The first number indicates how dustproof a light is on a scale of 1 to 5. The second number is water resistance. A number between 1 and 6 indicates a product is water-resistant, and 7 or 8 means it’s waterproof. Most of the lights on this list are either a 5 or 6 for being dustproof, and although they are all water-resistant, none are waterproof. Because these lights are charged by the rays of the sun, keeping them dust-free and keeping your gutters clean will directly influence the effectiveness of these lights.

It’s also important to note that while many of the lights claim to work at least 8 hours after a day of charging, cold weather can affect how well they stay charged. Therefore, these lights may perform for shorter periods, closer to 6 hours, when used during the winter or in cooler climates.

Most of the best solar gutter lights will automatically turn on when their built-in photosensors recognize that it’s getting dark. The length of time they run for, or their operating time, will vary depending on battery size, light output, and how much sun each light receives during a given day. Most of the lights we tested required 6 to 8 hours of charging time to last an average of 8 hours in the night, with some able to run as long as 10 to 12 hours.

Solar gutter lights have onboard batteries that charge using energy from the sun, similar to those found on solar chargers. The light absorbs solar energy via a built-in photovoltaic cell. The cell then converts the energy into electricity and stores it in the battery. For some of the lights, the battery is a built-in component, but others take a rechargeable AA battery. This battery is most often included with the lights and may need to be replaced every 12 months to 3 years, depending on manufacturer’s recommendation and how much weather the lights have endured.

Battery power output can vary between 800 and up to 3,000 milliamp hours, and the larger the battery, the more energy it can produce. The panel’s size relative to the battery’s size determines how efficiently the light will charge. Too large a cell and the battery will fill too quickly, wasting sunlight. Too small and a battery may never reach its full potential. For this reason, most manufacturers try to size their photovoltaic cells to match their output ratings.

Choosing the best solar gutter lights for your home might come down to ease of installation. Many of these models simply attach to the lip of a home’s gutters, tightening down onto the edge. All that’s required to secure them is a ladder and a pair of pliers or a screwdriver, depending on the model.

Other models might require the user to attach them directly to the home’s structure with brackets and screws. While this could seem like an inconvenience, these models typically have the greatest light output and battery life, so there is a trade-off. Installing these lights typically requires a ladder, a power drill, and a screwdriver.

In general, most solar lights are function first, meaning they may not add to a home’s curb appeal. But, there are models available that aren’t as jarring to the eye. For the most part, gutters on homes are white, so most gutter lights are available in white plastic. Homes with gutters in other colors might look better with black solar gutter lights, which are readily available.

If you’re unable to find a light that matches well with your home’s aesthetic, you can still achieve attractive outdoor lighting by finding a model that attaches directly to the home’s structure. This allows them to be hidden under the eave somewhat, but it’s important that they get at least some sunlight to function as expected.

Some additional features help increase the convenience and functionality of the best solar gutter lights. For example, a motion sensor might activate when it senses someone or something walking underneath it, which is excellent for security.

Many models also come with automatic switches that activate the light once a sensor determines it’s getting dark. And should the battery still have enough charge by morning, the controller will turn the light off when the sun comes up. There are also models with remote controls, which allow you to operate the lights remotely and adjust their output without climbing a ladder.

If you still have some questions about the best solar gutter lights, this section is for you. It’s a collection of some of the most frequently asked questions about solar gutter lights. Be sure to check for an answer to your question below.

Solar lights work best when the light is most available. While solar gutter lights are weatherproof and designed for year-round use, it’s important to remember that heavy snowfall can break and damage gutters, and also the lights.

Solar gutter lights typically come with everything necessary for setup and use.

There are solar lights that produce as much as 1,500 lumens of brightness.

Most solar lights are not motion activated, but there are solar lights that have motion-activated features.

If properly cared for, many solar gutter lights can last for years. Manufacturers frequently offer a 1-year warranty on gutter lights, but this can vary depending on the product, material, and type of weather the lights may endure.

#7803. Winter Container Inspiration From New Jersey

Hi GPOD! Today we’re returning to New Jersey to see more from Ellen Goldfarb and Tracy Buttrick. After sharing their beautiful fall containers with us, Ellen is back with some winter inspiration using colorful branches, evergreens, berries, pinecones, and more.

This beautiful antique lead planter in Ridgewood, New Jersey, always calls for a generous amount of greenery and nice height. We try to change what we do from year to year. This time we used curly willow, artificial white berry picks, magnolia leaves, red winterberry (Ilex verticillata, Zones 3–9), and frosted pinecones. Silver bell eucalyptus, silver brunia stems, noble fir (Abies procera, Zones 5–6), and incense cedar (Calocedrus decurrens, Zones 5–8) fill out the arrangement.

This is the same antique planter and house as in the previous photo, but from another winter. That year we used a combination of yellow twig dogwood (Cornus sericea ‘Flaviramea’, Zones 3–7) and red twig dogwood (Cornus sericea cvs., Zones 2–7) for lots of winter color. We also used artificial berry picks in pink and white and natural brown pine cones.

We like to use real berries, but sometimes the birds eat them before the season ends. Artificial berries give the client guaranteed color for longer. For greenery, we used desert juniper (Juniperus osteosperma, Zones 3–9), balsam fir (Abies balsamea, Zones 3–6), and incense cedar.

This slim planter sits on a small sliver of a step at an entry in Ho-Ho-Kus, New Jersey. It is simple but one of my favorites, with stunning red twig dogwood stems. We buy these from a farm that also grows and sells the more common darker-red stems.

Beneath the red is a froth of desert juniper. Dried lotus pods (Nelumbo cvs., Zones 4–10) and clusters of silver brunia punctuate the greenery. The finishing touch is a frilly skirt of bright chartreuse incense cedar.

This one sounds like an outfit, doesn’t it?

One of a pair of pots on the front porch of a Mission-style house in Teaneck, New Jersey, these had plenty of space for tall branches. We liked the combination of golden curly willow (Salix matsudana ‘Tortuosa’, Zones 4–8) and redtwig dogwood against the creamy tan stucco.

We tucked in shiny magnolia leaves with taller silver bell eucalyptus, then added natural brown pinecones and small clumps of silver brunia. A generous, draping swath of incense cedar finishes the bottom of the arrangement.

This is a window box in Englewood, New Jersey. A classic house calls for a classic planting. We used red winterberries, magnolia leaves, frosted pinecones, and silver brunia clusters. Some noble fir and our favorite evergreen, incense cedar, finish the arrangement.

This is a close-up detail of a planter in Franklin Lakes, New Jersey. Dark red twig dogwood stems are mixed with curly willow and branches of multiflora rose hips. We love using the rose hips, but they are sometimes hard to find.

This pot also had artificial white berry picks and Eastern white pine (Pinus strobus, Zones 3–8). Silver brunia on longer stems, noble fir, and incense cedar complete the arrangement.

Thank you for sharing more of your beautiful container designs with us, Ellen and Tracy! I love seeing how many different looks can come from a relatively small palette of winter materials. Changing the color and shape of the branches, berries, cones, and evergreens gives each container its own personality.

We have even more of Ellen and Tracy’s winter containers to share, so we’ll be back tomorrow with another round of inspiration!

#7801. Winter Container Designs from Ellen and Tracy

Hi everyone! I hope you’re enjoying the cool weather and a nice cup of coffee—or seven. With winter right around the corner, I’ve been absolutely gushing over these container designs from New Jersey garden designers Ellen Goldfarb and Tracy Buttrick of What’s Blooming. The wheels are turning! Here’s another round of their winter container designs to inspire us.

These sturdy, no-nonsense planters stand guard on either side of an impressive entry in Saddle River, New Jersey. The challenge here is matching the weight of the pots and doors. We had to carefully avoid the glass lamps just above them.

We carefully placed birch logs and then filled around them with some golden curly willow (Salix matsudana ‘Tortuosa’, Zones 4–8) and berried Chinese juniper (Juniperus chinensis, Zones 4–9). The red berries are winterberry (Ilex verticillata, Zones 3–9). Greens are a bit of desert juniper (Juniperus osteosperma, Zones 3–9), noble fir (Abies procera, Zones 5–6), and incense cedar (Calocedrus decurrens, Zones 5–8). We also used frosted pine cones, some lotus pods (Nelumbo cvs., Zones 4–10), and silver brunia.

Close-up of one of the planters in the previous picture

Another pot at the same house in Saddle River: This one sits at the front door, where we had the same challenge. We were working with chunky planters, limited porch space, impressive doors, and breakable lamps above.

We opted for thick bunches of redtwig dogwood (Cornus sericea cvs., Zones 2–7) against the off-white stone walls. We added lots of desert juniper, red winterberries, natural brown pine cones, some silver bell eucalyptus, noble fir, and incense cedar.

This pot and its twin on the other side of the door and landing stand in front of the one in the previous picture, but down one step. You can see a peek of the red branches in the background.

For contrast with the red planter in back, we used cooler colors: yellow twig dogwood (Cornus sericea ‘Flaviramea’, Zones 3–7), artificial white berries, and frosted pine cones. Finally, we added clusters of silver brunia, noble fir branches, and incense cedar.

A small planter on a covered porch in Saddle River, New Jersey, is crowned with southern magnolia (Magnolia grandiflora, Zones 6–10) leaves. Pieces of incense cedar peek through here and there. We love using seeded eucalyptus, and that year we found really pretty purple branches of it. Some natural brown pine cones and clusters of silver brunia complete the planting.

The tall branches are white-painted “sweet huck” branches (huckleberry) mixed with dark redtwig dogwood. Under them are branches of seeded eucalyptus and red winterberries, some frosted pine cones, a little noble fir, and incense cedar.

Thanks for another dose of winter container inspiration, Ellen and Tracy! It’s been such a joy to see your designs—you are both incredible artists.

And we’ll be back tomorrow for another round of winter containers. Hopefully you’ve spotted something you’d like to try or re-create in your own containers this season!

#7800. One More Round of Winter Container Inspiration

Hi everyone! Before we jump in, a quick note: We had a little technical hiccup today, and our GPOD didn’t publish when it was supposed to. If you missed it, you can catch up on Ellen Goldfarb and Tracy Buttrick’s winter container designs here.

Now, let’s finish out the week with one more round of winter inspiration from Ellen and Tracy of What’s Blooming! I hope these containers have given you plenty of ideas to play around with in your own seasonal displays.

This cedar-shake square pot in Tenafly, New Jersey, is one of a pair flanking the steps of this rustic porch. It is under the roof, so the artificial cardinals won’t disintegrate! For height, we used birch logs, some short stems of curly willow, and lots of silver bell eucalyptus.

The greens were desert juniper (Juniperus osteosperma, Zones 3–9), noble fir (Abies procera, Zones 5–6), and incense cedar (Calocedrus decurrens, Zones 5–8). Pine cones, both frosted and brown, and small bunches of silver brunia finished off the planter.

Close-up of a tall, stand-alone pot out in front of a house in Allendale, New Jersey: It can be seen from all sides. We used tall birch logs and tall stems of heavily berried Chinese juniper (Juniperus chinensis, Zones 4–9). Silver bell eucalyptus, small curly willow branches, frosted pine cones, silver brunia clusters, and incense cedar branches fill out the arrangement.

The owner of this house in Saddle River just loved red winterberries (Ilex verticillata, Zones 3–9), so we used lots of them! There was plenty of room for height, so we added tall curly willow, which contrasted nicely with the white background.

There are some tall Chinese juniper tucked in and rosettes of magnolia leaves with natural brown pine cones, silver brunia clusters, a little noble fir, and lots of incense cedar around the rim.

Here you can see the previous planter on the front porch with its partner.

Thanks so much to Ellen and Tracy for sharing this incredible collection of winter containers with us! Please continue to submit images of all the beautiful containers you create. I can only imagine what spring and summer look like!

Hopefully everyone found a new combination, material, or idea to try in their own containers this winter. Have a wonderful weekend, and we’ll see you back here on Monday!

#7798. GPOD on the Road: A Historic Garden Built for Two Sisters

In June 2022, I attended the Garden Club of Evanston’s Garden Walk. I toured several beautiful gardens and learned a bit about their histories, but one I still think about today is the historic sunken garden at the Bichl and Schager houses in nearby Wilmette, Illinois.

The story goes back to 1923, when sisters Helen Bichl and Dorothy Schager had neighboring homes built on their family’s property. Their father, Wendelin Seng, had established a successful furniture-hardware manufacturing business, and architects George W. Maher and his son Philip were commissioned to design the two Italianate-style homes. The houses were built with nearly identical, reversed floor plans and a shared garden connecting them. The original estate also included tennis courts, a swimming pool, and even an underground tunnel between the houses! You can read more about the fascinating history of these homes here.

This is one of the two historic homes. Many of the same plants repeat throughout this side of the garden, including Russian sage (Salvia yangii, Zones 5–9) on the slope near the stairs, clipped boxwood hedges (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9) lining the gravel paths, and roses (Rosa cvs., Zones 4–9) planted throughout the beds.

Here’s the second house. Both homes have beautiful stone terraces overlooking the garden. What a dream! This side has a greater mix of perennials and shrubs, but still repeats the formal boxwood hedges, roses, and gravel paths connecting the two homes.

A closer look at one of the planters next to the house. I thought the concrete urn really complemented the stonework.

Another view of the sunken garden. Photo 1 shows a staircase similar to the one in this photo, and both lead to the upper garden.

Woodland sage (Salvia nemorosa, Zones 4–8) and lady’s mantle (Alchemilla mollis, Zones 3–8) were a repeated combination throughout the gardens.

Looking back across the garden from near one of the staircases, you can see how densely planted the slopes are. Roses and flowering perennials fill the beds, and the clipped hedges maintain the garden’s formal structure. A work of art!

The upper garden. This angle faces the house in photo 1.

A shady spot to take a break from the June heat! I love how the astilbe (Astilbe cvs., Zones 4–8) foliage creeps beneath the bench here.

A gorgeous stone wall covered in creeping sedum (Sedum cvs., Zones 3–9) and a weathered birdbath. This is on the right side of the staircase in photo 4.

Another surprise in the upper garden was this waterfall tucked beneath the evergreens.

If you’re ever in the Evanston area, I highly recommend attending one of the Garden Club of Evanston’s garden walks. It’s a wonderful opportunity to explore beautiful private gardens and learn a little about their history. I’m certainly glad I had the chance to visit this one!

#7797. November 7 as Victims of Communism Day - 2026

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I have long advocated using May 1 for this purpose. But November 7 is a worthy alternative candidate, which I am happy to adopt if it can attract a broad consensus.

NOTE: The following post is largely adapted from last year's November 7 post on the same subject.

Since 2007, I have advocated designating May 1 as an international Victims of Communism Day. The May 1 date was not my original idea. But I have probably devoted more time and effort to it than any other commentator. In my view, May 1 is the best possible date for this purpose because it is the day that communists themselves used to celebrate their ideology, and because it is associated with communism as a global phenomenon, not with any particular communist regime. However, I have also long recognized that it might make sense to adapt another date for Victims of Communism Day, if it turns out that some other date can attract a broader consensus behind it. The best should not be the enemy of the good.

As detailed in my May 1 post from 2019, November 7 is probably the best such alternative, and over time it has begun to attract considerable support. Unlike May 1, this choice is unlikely to be contested by trade unionists and other devotees of the pre-Communist May 1 holiday. While I remain unpersuaded by their objections on substantive grounds, pragmatic considerations suggest that an alternative date is worth considering, if it can  thereby attract broader support.

The November 7 option is not without its own downsides. From an American standpoint, one obvious one is that it will often fall close to election day. On such occasions, a November 7 Victims of Communism Day might not attract as much attention as it deserves, because many will - understandably - be focused on electoral politics instead. Nonetheless, November 7 remains the best available alternative to May 1; or at least the best I am aware of.

For that reason, I am once again  doing a Victims of Communism Day post on November 7, in addition to the one I do on May 1. If November 7 attracts more support, I may eventually switch to that date exclusively. But, for now, I reserve the options of returning to an exclusive focus on May 1, doing annual posts on both days, or switching to some third option should a good one arise.

In addition to its growing popularity, November 7 is a worthy alternative because it is the anniversary of the day that the very first communist regime was established in Russia. All subsequent communist regimes were at least in large part inspired by it, and based many of their institutions and policies on the Soviet model.

The Soviet Union did not have the highest death toll of any communist regime. That dubious distinction belongs to the People's Republic of China. North Korea probably surpassed the USSR in the sheer extent of totalitarian control over everyday life. Pol Pot's Cambodia may have surpassed it in terms of the degree of sadistic cruelty and torture practiced by the regime, though this is admittedly very difficult to measure. But all of these tyrannies - and more - were at least to a large extent variations on the Soviet original.

Having explained why November 7 is worthy of consideration as an alternative date, it only remains to remind readers of the more general case for having a Victims of Communism Day. The following is adopted from this year's May 1 Victims of Communism Day post, and some of its predecessors:

The Black Book of Communism estimates the total at 80 to 100 million dead, greater than that caused by all other twentieth century tyrannies combined. We appropriately have a Holocaust Memorial Day. It is equally appropriate to commemorate the victims of the twentieth century's other great totalitarian tyranny.

Our comparative neglect of communist crimes has serious costs. Victims of Communism Day can serve the dual purpose of appropriately commemorating the millions of victims, and diminishing the likelihood that such atrocities will recur. Just as Holocaust Memorial Day and other similar events promote awareness of the dangers of racism, anti-Semitism, and radical nationalism, so Victims of Communism Day can increase awareness of the dangers of left-wing forms of totalitarianism, and government domination of the economy and civil society.

While communism is most closely associated with Russia, where the first communist regime was established, it had comparably horrendous effects in other nations around the world. The highest death toll for a communist regime was not in Russia, but in China. Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward was likely the biggest episode of mass murder in the entire history of the world.

November 7, 2017 was the 100th anniversary of the Bolshevik seizure of power in Russia, which led to the establishment of the first-ever communist regime. On that day, I put up a post outlining some of the lessons to be learned from a century of experience with communism.  The post explains why the lion's share of the horrors perpetrated by communist regimes were inherent flaws  of the system. For the most part, they cannot be ascribed to circumstantial factors, such as flawed individual leaders, peculiarities of Russian and Chinese culture, or the absence of democracy. Some of these other factors, especially the last, probably did make the situation worse than it might have been otherwise. But, for reasons I explained in the same post, some form of dictatorship is  virtually inevitable in a socialist economic system where the government controls all or nearly all of the economy.

While the influence of communist ideology has declined since its mid-twentieth century peak, it is far from dead. Largely unreformed communist regimes remain in power in Cuba and North Korea. In Venezuela, the Marxist government's policies have resulted in political repression, the starvation of children, and a massive refugee crisis - the biggest in the history of the Western hemisphere. The removal of President Nicolas Maduro has so far done little to change the nature of that regime.

In Russia, the authoritarian regime of former KGB Colonel Vladimir Putin has embarked on a wholesale whitewashing of communism's historical record. Putin's brutal and indefensible invasion of Ukraine owes more to Russian nationalist ideology than communism. But it is nonetheless fed in part by his desire to recapture the supposed power and glory of the Soviet Union, and his long-held belief that the collapse of the USSR was "the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the century." It is also telling that most communists in Russia and elsewhere have joined with nationalists in backing Putin's line on the war.

In China, the Communist Party remains in power (albeit after having abandoned many of its previous socialist economic policies), and has recently become less tolerant of criticism of the mass murders of the Mao era (part of a more general turn towards greater repression).

China's horrific repression of the Uighur minority is reminiscent of similar policies under Mao and Stalin, though it has not - so far - reached the level of actual mass murder. But imprisoning over 1 million people in horrific concentration camps is more than bad enough.

Far-left support for Hamas since the horrific October 7, 2023 terrorist attack is yet another reminder of the inherently evil nature of communist ideology. Backing terrorism is part of a long history of support for repression and mass murder. Not all extreme socialists of the type who support Hamas are communists. But the latter are a subset of the former.

In the West, the popularity of "democratic socialism" in some quarters is a sign that many have failed to learn the lessons of the communist experience. Democratic socialism has many of the same flaws as its authoritarian counterpart, and - as the Venezuelan case shows -  is unlikely to stay democratic for long, if implemented. Ironically, in their support for sweeping government control of the economy, democratic socialists have much in common with MAGA nationalists.

Victims of Communism Day is also a good time to remember our duty to help those victims. Among other things, it is unjust to deport migrants fleeing oppressive Marxist dictatorships, like those Cuba, Nicaragua and Venezuela, as the Trump Administration seeks to do to hundreds of thousands who entered the US legally under the CNVH program. This year, Trump ramped up efforts to deport Cubans back to their communist oppressors.If some on the left tend to ignore the evils of socialism, many on the nationalist right have been exacerbating the plight of its victims.

In sum, we need Victims of Communism Day because we have never given sufficient recognition to the victims of the modern world's most murderous ideology or come close to fully appreciating the lessons of this awful era in world history. In addition, that ideology, and variants thereof, still have a substantial number of adherents in many parts of the world, and still retains considerable intellectual respectability even among many who do not actually endorse it. Just as Holocaust Memorial Day serves as a bulwark against the reemergence of fascism, so this day of observance can help guard against the only ideology with an even greater number of victims.

#7796. Spring in Susan’s Minnesota Garden

Hi GPODers! We’re heading back to St. Paul, Minnesota, today for another look at Susan Warde’s garden. We’ve already followed Susan’s garden from late summer into fall and then looked back at spring and summer. This time, Susan is taking us back even further to April and May, when the garden was just getting going.

Large-flowered bellwort (Uvularia grandiflora, Zones 3–8), April 26. This is a Minnesota native. It spreads enthusiastically via seeds and rhizomes. Siberian squill (Scilla siberica, Zones 2–8), which earlier formed a solid blue carpet, is winding down.

Tarda tulip (Tulipa urumiensis, Zones 3–8), April 26. It’s not at all “tardy” and flowers well before the horticultural varieties. This little naturalizer forms large, cheerful patches. Its one drawback is that it only opens in sunshine.

April 29. I love the pattern and color combinations here. The upper plant is ‘Green Spice’ heuchera (Heuchera ‘Green Spice’, Zones 4–9). The lower one is red trillium (Trillium recurvatum, Zones 4–9). It was a gift from a friend and languished for a number of years in its original tucked-away spot. Three years ago I moved it, and it has flourished. Like the trillium below, it’s a spring ephemeral that eventually dies back to the ground.

Large-flowered trillium (Trillium grandiflorum, Zones 4–8), May 2. It provides a food source for early pollinators (note the little bee in the lowest flower). I have various clumps of this in the shadier back garden, but obviously it doesn’t seem to mind several hours of morning sun.

Japanese primrose (Primula sieboldii, Zones 3–8), May 8. This is one of my favorites in spite of the fact that its foliage starts looking pretty disreputable as the season progresses. It spreads like crazy but is easily transplanted or pulled up. I had also purchased the much less vigorous white variety, which died out. Then a few years later it appeared again, presumably from seed, and I have coddled it into three diminutive clumps.

‘Cherry Garden’, a standard dwarf bearded iris (Iris ‘Cherry Garden’, Zones 3–9), May 8. This is a very vigorous little iris, purchased from the same nursery as the Japanese primroses.

I particularly enjoy seeing GPOD photos that show more than one or two single plants, so here’s a general view of the front garden (May 8) for those who feel as I do. The garden goes virtually all the way up to the neighbors’ house on the left.

In the foreground are bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos spectabilis, Zones 3–9) and a small clump of Virginia bluebells (Mertensia virginica, Zones 3–8) that seems to have escaped from the back garden. The large trunk on the left and the pink-flowered tree in the background are ‘Red Splendor’ crabapples (Malus ‘Red Splendor’, Zones 3–8). They are now no longer in the garden, having been taken down in September (but that’s another story).

The tree with the reddish foliage (upper center) is a Japanese-Korean hybrid, ‘North Wind’ (Acer × pseudosieboldianum ‘North Wind’, Zones 4–7). There are two other Japanese-Korean hybrids in the photo, ‘Ice Dragon’ on the right and ‘Alpen Glow’ on the left. The latter was new this spring. It’s gorgeous in the spring and has now turned a pretty orangey red, but I found its summer foliage color disappointing, a rather dull brownish green.

General view of the back garden, May 9. ‘North Wind’ and ‘Ice Dragon’ maples are pictured here, along with an actual, less hardy Japanese maple (Acer palmatum ‘Emperor I’, Zones 5–8). It has now survived its first winter in my garden (and so, giddy with success, I recently planted another where the back crabapple was taken down). I love its early red color that echoes the red stems on emerging ferns.

Here is ‘Cherry Garden’ again, May 14, along with another clump of the ubiquitous Japanese primrose. I don’t know the name of the heuchera that also surrounds the sundial, having acquired it from someone selling plants out of his garden (long before jumping worms became a worry). It produces stalks of tiny white blossoms that continue sporadically throughout the summer.

The narrow bluish leaves in the lower left belong to curly onion (Allium senescens ‘Glaucum’, Zones 4–8), which won’t bloom until late in the season. In the lower right you can see prairie smoke (Geum triflorum, Zones 3–7) in flower, a vigorous grower like the other four plants featured here.

May 24, front garden. In the foreground is a ‘Northern Hi-Lights’ azalea (Rhododendron ‘Northern Hi-Lights’, Zones 4–7), hardy down to –40°F. (My only winter worry about it is not low temperatures but rabbits…) That’s another ‘North Wind’ maple in the background.

Thanks for taking us even further back into your garden, Susan! It’s so much fun seeing how quickly the garden changes from those first April blooms to the much fuller landscape just a few weeks later. And I’m with you on the wider garden views. It’s always nice to see how all these individual plants come together!

Have photos to share? We’d love to see your garden, a particular collection of plants you love, or a wonderful garden you had the chance to visit!

To submit, fill out the Garden Photo of the Day Submission Form.

You can also send 5–10 photos to [email protected] along with some information about the plants in the pictures and where you took the photos. We’d love to hear where you are located, how long you’ve been gardening, successes you are proud of, failures you learned from, hopes for the future, favorite plants, or funny stories from your garden.

#7795. Attorney Fee Award Cut from $100K to $50K, Partly as Sanction for Hallucinated Citations

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

In Ellis v. McNeese, written by Kansas District Court Judge W. Lee Fowler (decided April 22 but just posted on Westlaw), plaintiff's lawyer prevailed in getting his client reinstated as a nursing student who was punished by Flint Hills Technical College for a religiously motivated vaccine refusal. But when it came to getting attorney fees (which are allowed by the Kansas Preservation of Religious Freedom Act), the lawyer fared worse. The court concluded, for various reasons, that the lawyer would normally have been entitled to $100K in fees rather than the $300K he claimed, but then it went on to reduce the fees even further:

On October 20, 2025, Plaintiff's counsel filed a document entitled Opposition to Defendants Motion to Alter Judgment. Within that pleading the Plaintiff's counsel falsely cited two cases, State v. Baker, 290 Kan. 842, 235 P.3d 424 (2010) and Gannon v. State, 298 Kan. 110 310 P.3d 1196 (2014) for propositions of legal authority that are inconsistent with the case cited. In addition, there were no fewer than six false citations to non-existent Kansas case law. When confronted by these misrepresentations and facing a Motion for Sanctions, Plaintiff's counsel did not deny the allegations or explain how he came up with the false citations, he simply responded that the legal propositions contained in his pleadings were accurate and that his "citation irregularities were technical and clerical…".

Citations to non-existent cases can never be considered technical or clerical errors. They are not formatting or citation errors. They are unprofessional and sanctionable. This Court suspects that Plaintiff's counsel used a generative artificial intelligence program as an aid in drafting his pleading, but no such admission was forthcoming from counsel. Counsel's response to the claim for sanctions is simply the proposition of "no harm, no foul". In addition, this is not the only time Plaintiff's counsel has submitted false citations to a district court. See Anderson v. Aldrich, Douglas County District Court Case No. DG-2025-CV-429, Memorandum Opinion dated March 13, 2026.

Kansas District Court judges must rely on the veracity of citations presented to the court by counsel. The timeline for making decisions at the district court level is measured in minutes, hours, or days. We do not have law clerks to review pleadings for citation errors or misrepresentations. We must rely on attorneys to act professionally in preparing and filing pleadings to be considered by the Court. Plaintiff's actions have failed in that regard. In addition, those actions appear to violate Rule 3.3 of the Code of Professional Responsibility. (The actual adjudication of such a violations a matter for determination by the Kansas Board for Discipline of Attorneys.)

In addition, this Court held a status or pretrial conference in this case on January 29, 2026, for the purpose of preparing for the trial of the attorney fees claim. Defense counsel prepared a proposed journal entry for that hearing which did include the recitation of orders made by the court on pending garnishment proceedings. On January 30, 2026, Plaintiff's counsel filed objections to the proposed journal entry and then proceeded to file a journal entry prepared by Plaintiff's counsel representing that it had been approved by defense counsel. Plaintiff's counsel did not have the consent to file said journal entry. The factual scenario is set forth in the Defendant's Motion for Relief from Order filed on January 30, 2026. It is incorporated herein by reference.

Not only was the presentation of the proposed journal entry a violation of Rule 170 as it applies to the filing of journal entries, Plaintiff's counsel's action appears to be an additional violation of Rule 3.3 of the Code of Professional Responsibility by representing opposing counsel's approval when it had not been obtained. The Court vacated the offending journal entry by Memorandum Decision on February 2, 2026. On March 12, 2026, the Court approved and filed the journal entry for said hearing.

District court judges need to rely on counsels' representations on approvals for journal entries submitted in the e-file system. Often that approval is designated by a /S/ symbol on the signature line. It is not unusual to receive 20 or 30 documents per day for review and approval. In fact, some dockets in this district can result in filings more than 100 on any given day. Many of these documents come in days after the hearing. Strict compliance with Rule 170 is mandatory and not an option….

Plaintiff's counsel initially did a good job representing his client and got the relief she needed to finish school and graduate on time…. As previously noted, this Court's calculation of the attorney fee award was initially set at $101,640.00.

However, this Court is of the opinion that it is appropriate to strike 50% of that fee as a sanction for Plaintiff's falsifications of citations and misrepresentations noted above. The Plaintiff is awarded the sum of $50,820.00 for her attorney fees incurred herein. Judgment shall be entered in favor of Plaintiff for that amount.

Although this sanction may seem substantial to some, Plaintiff's counsel breached the bond of trust that the Court imposes on attorneys in their professional capacity as officers of the court….. The Court further finds that the Clerk of the District Court is directed to provide a copy of this Memorandum Order to the Kansas Board of Profession Responsibility for their consideration….

An appeal is pending; you can read plaintiff's lawyer's brief as to the fees here.

#7794. The Best Space Heaters of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Stacey L. Nash, Tom Scalisi, Additional research provided by Glenda Taylor

Published Nov 6, 2026 9:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Ever-rising utility costs can make heating an entire house prohibitively pricey, so to save money but still keep occupied areas comfortable, many renters and homeowners take advantage of space heaters. Today’s models offer basic heating features at more affordable prices, convenient bells and whistles, and upgraded safety features. To help you choose the model with the aspects you want most, we put 11 space heaters through a series of hands-on tests.

Testing took place in real-life scenarios to put performance and safety features on the spot and to give us an inside look at how each model functioned over time. We also spoke to Robin Saidov, an energy industry expert, electrical engineer, and the owner of Your Energy Footprint, a company in Westport, Connecticut, that educates consumers on ways to be more energy efficient. Based on our tests and Robin’s advice, we chose the Amazon Basics Portable Manual-Control Radiator Heater as our top pick for its easy assembly, noiseless operation, and ample heat. Below, learn what we found, how to navigate the options, and why the models below are among the best space heaters available.

Bottom line: Space heaters offer cost-effective warmth with enhanced safety features. Choose the right model based on room size and energy efficiency for the best results.

A space heater can be a welcome source of supplemental warmth in a chilly room, especially if it also saves money on utility costs by allowing the user to turn the HVAC thermostat down a few degrees. Keep in mind that space heaters get very hot and, if used carelessly, they can lead to a house fire. Before looking for a space heater, it’s a good idea for shoppers to call their homeowners insurance agent, since some insurance policies will not cover damages from a fire caused by a space heater.

To qualify as a top pick, a space heater needed to show in our testing that it was powerful enough to heat the intended room. We also made sure each included safety features that would turn the unit off if it fell over. The following models are suited to various heating needs, and any one of them might well serve a variety of situations.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Performance 3/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 4/5; Value 4/5

The Amazon Basics portable manual-control radiator heater is aptly named, as it is a basic space heater. This oil-filled radiator features two control knobs (temperature and output) for setting the heater and letting it do its work, so it is very easy to use.

This model features a 1,500W output, allowing it to heat large rooms. It also features a tip-over switch and overheat protection for safety, and it operates nearly silently, aside from the sound of an air bubble in the oil now and then. It measures 26.38 inches tall (with wheels) by 13.19 inches wide by 9.84 inches deep. It features a top-mounted handle for transport as well, and it weighs 15.41 pounds.

There isn’t a lot to say about the Amazon Basics oil heater. It was easy to assemble and use, and it produced plenty of heat (although it took 2 hours to heat a living room from 60 to 70 degrees Fahrenheit). There isn’t a digital display or remote control to adjust the temperature, but the fact that it provides silent heat is really a plus—all that’s discernible is a click every now and then when the heating element kicks on and off. It might be a little too simple for tech lovers, however.

Get the Amazon Basics space heater at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Performance 4/5; Noise 3/5; Portability 5/5; Value 5/5

For a reasonable price, this oscillating heater provides 1,500 watts of heat, enough to keep a 150-square-foot room warm and cozy. It features three power outputs (low, high, and fan only), plus tip-over shutoff for safety should it inadvertently get knocked over. There’s a simple on/off switch for easy operation and a thermostat dial that allows the user to select the desired temperature. After the user sets the thermostat, the heater will turn itself on and off to maintain the selected temperature. It weighs a mere 3.2 pounds and boasts a handle on the back for easy toting from room to room.

While this simple heater did well during testing, it doesn’t have any features that make it stand out. The basic heat functions worked well, and the adjustable thermostat triggered an automatic shutoff. However, it could use a display to show the exact temperature setting. The current variable thermostat left us guessing as to the temperature we were choosing. Overall, it’s lightweight, portable, and made quick work of heating a 150-square-foot office.

Get the Amazon Basics oscillating space heater at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Performance 4/5; Noise 3/5; Portability 3/5; Value 4/5

For warmth and peace of mind, consider the ample safety features of the AirNmore Comfort Deluxe infrared space heater. Though it will heat a room up to 150 square feet, its outer casing will remain cool to the touch, which is crucial for homes with kids and pets. The tip-over safety function shuts the unit off if it gets knocked over, but since it weighs 22 pounds, this is a less likely scenario than with some smaller models. A 14-gauge cord with a three-prong heater plug reduces the risk of the cord melting from overheating.

The power level is adjustable, and the heater has a built-in thermostat to maintain a consistent temperature. A removable, washable filter prevents dust from recirculating in the air. Users might mistake this space heater for an old-time radio; it definitely looks more design-friendly than some other more utilitarian models. We loved this heater in testing, although with infrared heaters, users have to direct the heat toward themselves. It’s a penetrating heat, but only if it hits the body.

A tiny remote control let us change modes (low or high) and temperatures while working at a desk, and we liked that we could precisely adjust the temperature setting and see it on the display. The downside with this AirNmore space heater is its size. It’s big and takes up a lot of room while heating up a relatively small 150-square-foot space. However, the casters make moving this behemoth out of the way when not in use fairly easy.

Get the AirNmore space heater at Amazon or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Performance 5/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 4/5; Value 5/5

This electric heater from Lasko’s Designer series has smooth contours and rests on an attractive base so that it looks more like a work of art than a space heater. Appearance aside, the ceramic model effectively heats rooms up to 150 square feet by oscillating smoothly from side to side for uniform heat distribution. Switch between its adjustable heat settings via the remote; the Lasko can even be programmed in advance to turn on and off when desired. This handsome space heater also features a safety shutoff in case the unit tips over.

This beauty was a pleasant surprise during testing because it cranks out the heat. It might be designed to heat 150-square-foot spaces, but it can do more than that with the heat it puts out. The oscillating setting spread the heat far and wide, quickly warming our 200-square-foot test space (another office) to perfection. We liked that we could pick the temperature setting, though it only goes in 5 degree Fahrenheit increments. Plus, it comes with a timer that automatically turns the unit off after 1, 2, or 4 hours. With that set, we didn’t worry about leaving it on while we were away.

Once the room reaches the set temperature, this space heater automatically shuts off. However, we noticed that if the temperature began to fall, it didn’t automatically turn back on. But we could turn it back on using the remote, so no one actually had to get out of their chair. This model might have made us a little lazy.

Get the Lasko space heater at Amazon or Best Buy.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Performance 5/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 3/5; Value 4/5

This 1,500-watt portable space heater from Dr. Infrared Heater looks like a classic radio but runs like the high-tech space heater that it is. Emitting only 39 decibels, this infrared heater features quiet air circulation that moves the heat through large spaces. We tested it in a 200-square-foot office, and this space heater made quick work of warming it. Infrared heaters don’t heat the air; instead, they heat objects. This heater’s quiet fan made it feel like the heat permeated farther and made a difference in overall room temperature.

It’s also packed with features including standby, eco, low, and high power modes. The digital display shows the thermostat’s setting, which makes it easy to make adjustments based on comfort levels.

We’re big fans of remote controls. This model’s remote control allowed us to make comfort adjustments without getting out of our office chair. We appreciated that we could leave it on all day while we worked, and it would turn on and off as needed. There’s also an adjustable timer, which can go up to 12 hours before automatically shutting off the heater.

Overall, it’s a nice-looking heater that can handle spaces up to about 850 square feet. It’s not the most mobile unit, weighing 24 pounds, but it does have casters for easier mobility.

Get the Dr. Infrared Heater space heater at Amazon, Lowe’s, The Home Depot, Walmart, or Dr. Heater.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Performance 4/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 5/5; Value 4/5

Figuring out the heat in a finished basement can be an ordeal but might be easily solved with the De’Longhi SlimStyle digital convection panel heater. This model can be set on the floor or mounted on the wall (the latter being best for basement duty), and it produces up to 1,500 watts of heating power. It measures 21.8 inches tall (with feet) by 32.2 inches wide by 8.5 inches deep.

The De’Longhi features a convection-style design that is virtually silent in three out of the four modes, and a fourth mode with a fan to help pump out the heat. It also features a fifth mode (anti-freeze), which the manufacturer says kicks on when the temperature in the space reaches 41 degrees Fahrenheit; this is to help prevent frozen pipes. The heater has a built-in tip-over switch as well as an overheat sensor, timers, and an electronic digital display. Unfortunately, it doesn’t come with a remote.

We’re not relegating the De’Longhi to the basement because it’s ugly; we honestly found it very nice looking. However, we think it’s best there for its included wall-mount brackets and the fact that it has a freeze-protection mode (ours activated at 45 degrees, not 41 like the manufacturer stated). With so many pipes and mechanicals in a finished basement, we thought this was the perfect solution to protect the investment. Also, most space heaters don’t reach settings that low, so this one works really well for that purpose.

There is one thing we couldn’t figure out, however: Why in the world doesn’t it come with a remote?

Get the De’Longhi SlimStyle space heater at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Performance 5/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 4/5; Value 4/5

The Heat Storm Logan Deluxe infrared heater is all about coziness. This powerful space heater features a 1,500W output, a digital display, and a remote control for managing the device from the couch. It has a faux-wood box-style design with fabric-covered sides, allowing it to blend in with comfortable living room decor. It can also handle large living rooms, considering it can warm up to 1,000 square feet.

This model features several modes—including high, medium, low, and auto—that control the heater based on the preset temperature. It also has a safe-touch exterior that remains cool and safe, a child lock, and overheat protection. The heater operates quietly (measured at 46 decibels on a sound meter app from about 4 feet away) as well. It measures 15.3 inches tall (with wheels) by 12.3 inches wide by 10.8 inches deep.

We’ll be honest and say that this heater has to match a living room decor to be a perfect fit, but if one of the three finish color options works, the unit can sit in the corner of any room and blend in until it’s needed.

While it’s light (10 pounds), the box itself is simply faux wood, which doesn’t seem as high in quality as other real-wood heaters that we’ve tested in the past. It had a better digital display than any of those other box-style heaters, however, and it produced a lot of heat, bringing a 63 degree Fahrenheit living room to 70 degrees Fahrenheit in about 15 minutes. Also, for those who care, it blows hot air out at the perfect height for one of our old dogs, who instantly laid down in front of it and fell asleep. We assume other four-legged friends will love it, too.

Get the Heat Storm Logan space heater at Amazon.

This space heater performed well in many respects. It has an adjustable thermostat, 11 heat settings, a cool-touch exterior, and a compact design. What it doesn’t have is an automatic tilt shut-off feature. That means if it gets knocked over, it keeps running. In a home with pets, kids, and, honestly, most adults, it could keep running face down, posing a fire hazard. For that reason, it didn’t make our list of top picks.

We tested these space heaters in person, in real-world situations. They were all tested in a home office setting where the office was 150 to 200 square feet in size. One of the test offices also had large windows, so the room temperature fluctuated more often. We tried them on different surfaces, from plush carpet to bare floors.

For models with a digital display, we set the thermostat between 70 and 75 degrees Fahrenheit to see how well the space heater kept a consistent room temperature. From there, we made adjustments to settings (low and high), timers, and safety features. For example, we tipped over every single space heater to make sure it turned off.

Models designed to turn on and off based on the thermostat were left running to see how they performed over time. Some stayed in standby mode for hours without turning on because a furnace kept the room at temperature. We wanted to make sure they wouldn’t turn on if it wasn’t necessary. Ease of use was also a consideration, and models with remote controls or intuitive designs got higher marks from us.

Besides taking into account the size of the room you’re planning to heat, Saidov says it’s a good idea to “find a model that has a set temperature.” She adds, “This will ensure that the unit doesn’t overheat the space.” She also says to make sure the space heater is Underwriters Laboratories (UL) certified, a third-party certification that means the heater meets certain safety standards. And, most importantly, “Electric space heaters should always be plugged into a wall outlet and grounded. Using extension cords and power strips can be a fire hazard.”

A small space heater might be suitable under a desk or next to a lounge chair, but it likely won’t make a dent in a sizable chilly room. A space heater’s size should suit the room that it will warm and should, of course, be as safe as possible.

For those just starting to shop, it might come as a surprise to find so many different types of heaters from which to choose. Each type has its pros and cons, and not all space heaters are suitable for all rooms and situations.

Fan space heaters function by heating the air around an electric coil or wire elements and then dispersing the heat with a fan. They are among the least expensive models but do not offer the same efficiency as other types. Therefore, fan heaters are best suited to rooms without drafts or for warming a small space quickly.

Convection space heaters warm air over ceramic plates or disks and allow it to radiate warmth into the room. Some models do include fans for quicker heat dispersal and, like conventional fan heaters, they work best in rooms without drafts. Convection heaters come in compact or tower models, often with exterior cases that are cooler to the touch. Prices vary depending on wattage and added features.

Infrared space heaters are among the quietest options for the home. They generate heat quickly by radiating heat to the objects—including people—in front of them. As opposed to heating the air in the room, this type of heater heats the user, making it a good choice for use in drafty rooms. All that’s needed is for the user to aim it directly at where they’re sitting.

Oil-filled space heaters (another type of radiant heater) are also a quiet option. Because they are capable of putting off an abundance of heat while using less electricity than fan-type models, these heaters are well suited to larger rooms. Due to the weight of the oil and the steel casing, these heaters are relatively heavy, but many come with wheels to make relocating easier. Oil-filled space heaters take a while to heat up, but they radiate continuously once they do.

Micathermic space heaters combine convection and radiant heating processes. Designed as a panel to stand or hang on a wall like a piece of artwork, they create a welcoming ambience for the senses by mimicking the look of a real fire and radiating heat. Some models include fans for greater efficiency and remote controls for extra convenience. These advanced heaters vary widely in price.

Space heaters are a leading cause of house fires, so the best space heaters boast safety features to reduce risk. Manufacturers have introduced automatic shutoffs that kick in when a unit overheats or gets inadvertently knocked over. In addition, many have exterior cases that keep units cool to the touch at all times. Some models even come equipped with motion sensors that automatically turn the heater off when a pet or child comes too close. For extra peace of mind when purchasing, look for the letters NRTL on the space heater packaging, which indicates that the model has been tested for safety by the Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory.

As a general rule of thumb, select a space heater that will produce 10 watts of power for every square foot. For instance, to heat a 12-foot-long by 10-foot-wide room, a shopper would need to purchase a 1,200W space heater. A very large room may require more than one space heater to maintain a comfortable temperature throughout.

Other factors that affect a space heater’s efficiency include ceiling height, the insulating factor of the exterior walls, the number of windows, and the available outlets. While high-wattage heaters offer more heat than lower-wattage models, they’re limited to the capacity of the electrical outlet; a home’s standard 110-volt electrical outlet can only provide 1,500W of power, so that must be the wattage cap for any machine plugged into it.

One of the main reasons for using a space heater is to save on energy costs. But unlike many other appliances, space heaters do not require energy testing by the Environmental Protection Agency, nor does the agency issue Energy Star ratings for them, so those who are serious about saving will want to opt for the most efficient type.

Oil-filled space heaters are among the most efficient because they heat the oil and the metal casing, gradually dispersing radiant warmth into the room. Once the oil reaches the desired temperature, less energy is needed to maintain that temperature. Even after an oil-filled heater is turned off, it will continue to radiate heat for up to 30 minutes or more. Next in energy efficiency are infrared space heaters, which use up to 10 percent less energy than space heaters with coils and fans.

For the most part, space heaters are among the quietest of all small appliances. Space heaters that use radiant heat, either infrared or oil-filled, make virtually no noise. Traditional space heaters with fans will emit an average of 35 to 45 decibels of sound, approximately the same as soft indoor conversation (which could be suitable to use as a white noise machine).

Homeowners and renters can save on utility costs by using a space heater in one or more rooms rather than heating the entire home. For the toastiest—and safest—results, check out these useful tips.

Most space heaters should be turned off at night and when you leave a room. The exception is an oil-filled radiating space heater, which can be left on. However, make certain not to leave anything flammable within 3 feet of the radiator.

Oil-filled radiant heaters use the least amount of electricity because once they heat up, it takes very little energy to keep them warm. Plus, they will radiate heat for up to 30 minutes or more after they’ve been turned off.

The safest space heater is one that will automatically shut off if it overheats or if it accidentally tips over.
