#7730. 31 Vintage Christmas Ideas Worth Bringing Back This Year

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 9, 2026 2:14 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Festive feather trees, classic cocktails, and decorative popcorn garlands: Yesteryear’s Christmas revelers really knew how to embrace the holiday season. This year, add a festive touch of seasonal cheer to your home with these old-school traditions. These vintage Christmas decorations and comforting treats will impress any guest, and create lasting memories for years to come.

Christmas teas aren’t just for the British. This traditional activity, which came to America in the 1830s as part of the temperance movement, brought families together to converse while drinking a variety of teas at long communal tables. So, fire up the tea kettle, make some fancy finger sandwiches, and enjoy a warm mug of tea with your loved ones.

The first artificial Christmas tree, which was a feather tree, dates back to mid-19th-century Germany. The thin-branched trees became popular in America in the 1920s, when European immigrants carried their holiday traditions to their new homes. Add a feather tree to your holiday decor for a touch of whimsy and historical charm.

Best Choice’s 9-foot tree has over 2,000 branch tips, strong branches, and beautiful flocking. Read the review.

Classic cocktails have made a comeback in bars around the country. Learn how to make a few favorites so you’ll have something to keep yourself warm, and impress your guests, over the holidays. Good choices for winter include the hot toddy (made with a bracing spirit like brandy, rum, or whiskey mixed with honey, spices, and boiling water) and the Tom and Jerry (a concoction of eggnog, brandy, and rum). Pouring your potables into fancy cocktail glasses makes them even more festive.

Jell-O long ago lost its spot as the star of the dessert table, but we think it’s about time the jiggly treat made a comeback. Pull out one of your grandma’s old recipe books and have fun constructing your very own holiday Jell-O mold, sure to be a crowd-pleaser at the kids’ table this year.

When families in the 1950s and ’60s didn’t want to maintain real Christmas trees, they opted for aluminum versions instead. Nowadays, these shimmering trees can add a little sparkly elegance to your seasonal decor while giving a nod to a long-lost trend. National Tree Company’s red tinsel tree is fire resistant, 6 feet high and has a 20-inch base diameter.

Before people adorned their trees with lights and ornaments, they decorated them with homemade popcorn garlands. Strings of popped kernels were budget-friendly and simple to construct. This year, spend quality time with your kids, parents, or grandparents making your own vintage popcorn garland. Be sure to pop extra corn to munch on as you work!

In the past, people traditionally thanked their regular letter carriers by giving them a small Christmas gift. Though we don’t always have the chance to develop relationships with our letter carriers today, it’s still a nice idea to give them a token of appreciation around the holidays. Just remember that federal guidelines stipulate that postal employees can’t accept gifts worth more than $20.

Stockings overflow with chocolates and toys on Christmas morning, but in simpler times children were excited and grateful to find oranges in their stockings. Put an orange in your child’s stocking this year as a reminder of your family’s good fortune, and for a healthy dose of vitamin C.

Tinsel became popular in the United States in the 1950s as people sought a way to add shimmer to their Christmas trees without using Christmas lights, which were considered a fire hazard. Re-create this vintage trend and give your tree a shiny, icy look by draping strands of tinsel on the branches. (Skip this tradition if you have pets, because tinsel is a choking hazard for them.)

With roots in solstice celebrations of ancient times, caroling is one of the oldest holiday traditions in the world. Channel your jolly ancestors and spread holiday cheer by taking your family Christmas caroling this year. Don’t worry if your singing voice doesn’t rival Beyoncé’s—this tradition is more about having fun than showing off your vocal chops.

In the early 20th century, people relied on trains as a primary mode of transportation. It’s no wonder that toy versions of these all-important vehicles started appearing underneath Christmas trees during that time. Set up a track around your Christmas tree to take your holiday visitors back in time, or gift a toy train to young relatives.

With the convenience of Netflix and DVDs, it’s easy to forget that children used to have to wait all year for their favorite classic Christmas specials to air on TV, and how excited they’d get when that day finally rolled around. Re-create the joys of a less plugged-in era by looking up the air times of old favorites, such as “A Charlie Brown Christmas,” or “How the Grinch Stole Christmas,” then whipping up a fresh batch of hot chocolate for a cozy night with the family.

Find a spot on the mantel for the classic figurines your family collected growing up, like Pixie Elves, Byers’ Choice Christmas Carolers, or Snowbabies. While the Elf on the Shelf might be the more common character right now, these guys were the original ones keeping watch over the house before Santa arrived.

If you don’t already have a Christmas village collection, consider starting one this year. The tradition of collecting miniature structures can be traced all the way back to the 17th century, but the charming ceramic houses and stores you know and love kicked off in the 1970s. Today, it’s easy to search up online sites and forums where Christmas village enthusiasts share their tips and tricks for creating elaborate setups.

We sing about it every year, but have you ever actually had a roasted chestnut? On a weekend afternoon or cozy evening, try your hand at roasting chestnuts—a stovetop will work just as well as an open fire for this.

Everything old is new again, and that includes ceramic Christmas trees. This ’70s Christmas decoration has roared back into style. If you don’t have one collecting dust in the basement, you can find the 15-inch Best Choice Products pre-lit ceramic Christmas tree, 18-inch Mr. Christmas ceramic tree, and others like them online.

If you have ever been to or seen photos of Dyker Heights Christmas lights, then you’re familiar with blow mold Christmas decorations. The playful plastic figurines first popped up on the market in the 1930s. Although many folks today like Christmas inflatables, we believe there’s enough room on the lawn for both.

Over the top, but worth it: BZB Goods’ Santa Claus with sleigh is 12 feet long and illuminated with internal lights.

While there are plenty of modern holiday hits to enjoy, set a retro mood by putting together a playlist with tracks from the likes of Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra. While music-streaming services like Spotify already have plenty of holiday playlists to choose from, you can also curate a selection that reminds you of Christmases past.

Snail mail is so retro! Virtual Christmas greetings get the job done, but they aren’t nearly as sentimental as old-fashioned handwritten cards. Crisp stationery and seasonal stamps never fail to spread holiday cheer. Buy a boxed card set, or take a picture with your kids (or pet!) and incorporate it into a personalized greeting for everyone on your mailing list.

While it’s convenient to pick up a freshly cut Christmas tree from a big-box store’s parking lot, the tradition doesn’t have quite the same sense of holiday magic as venturing into a snow-covered wood to choose the perfect type of Christmas tree for your home. Depending on where you live, there are likely Christmas tree farms in your area that allow you to choose and cut down your own Christmas tree.

In the Middle Ages, the Lord of Misrule was a figure who was appointed to take charge of planning the Christmas activities in royal courts and noble houses. But this tradition came with a twist: The “Lord” often planned holiday pranks and jests. Try out this historic practice in your home this holiday season by giving children turns being the Lord of Misrule for the day. Allow the “Lord” to decide which treats to eat after dinner, which holiday special to watch, or letting them arrange the Elf on the Shelf for the following day.

While today’s Christmas supper typically features turkey or ham as a main dish, goose was once the centerpiece of many holiday dinner tables. In fact, eating goose for Christmas is a tradition that dates back to ancient Greece. A goose may be tricky to track down, but it’s generally possible to order one in advance from a high-quality butcher.

Tiny warm white lights are most common nowadays—on the tree and outside—but why not decorate with some retro flair? The big, colorful light bulbs you remember from previous decades are now available ineco-friendly LED bulbs. The burst of color outlining your house will make your home stand out from everyone else’s on the block.

With 3-inch C9 LED bulbs, the indoor/outdoor C9 LED lights from Wintergreen 17-foot strings really dazzle when used to frame the roof,

Today, getting dressed up for Christmas dinner typically means showing up in pair of elastic-waist pants to accommodate second helpings of turkey. In photos of midcentury Christmases, however, you’ll likely see men in ties and women in chic dresses with nary a pair of sweatpants in sight. Update your holiday dress code this year to bring back some vintage holiday glamour.

Evoke a vintage Christmas vibe by watching some holiday classics this December. Introduce your family to some timeless black-and-white picks like Miracle on 34th Street, White Christmas, and It’s a Wonderful Life. If you’re already familiar with these classics, screen an underrated holiday flick like Christmas in Connecticut or I’ll Be Seeing You.

Christmas crackers first made an appearance in Victorian England and are still popular in the U.K., but aren’t common on American holiday tables. A cracker is a wrapped cardboard tube that makes a loud cracking sound when pulled at both ends. They typically contain paper crowns as well as a small trinket and a card containing a joke or a piece of trivia, all of which are great dinnertime icebreakers.

You’re probably familiar with the “12 Days of Christmas” tradition because of the popular yuletide carol, but it’s a tradition that has largely died out in North America. Christians traditionally celebrated from December 25 to January 5 or 6, and gave one another small gifts each day. Extend the holiday season in your home by keeping festivities alive until Twelfth Night and continue to enjoy Christmas treats and festive holiday movies.

Though in many ways Christmas has become commercialized, you can bring back the spirit of giving that the holiday season once held by lending a hand to your neighbors or community. Help an elderly neighbor hang Christmas lights, volunteer at a toy drive for underprivileged children, or spend a day working at a soup kitchen to spread holiday cheer to those who need it most.

The origin of bottle brush Christmas trees dates back to the 1940s when, as the story goes, Addis Housewares Company manufactured the trees on the same machines the company used to make toilet brushes. Addis never did confirm the truth of the tree’s manufacture, but we’ll never look at a toilet brush the same way again. Though vintage version of these faux-snow-covered trees are hard to come by, you can find reproductions at retailers like Target and Crate and Barrel.

#7729. The Butler Didn't Do It

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Todd Butler's bare Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire.

Todd Butler has now posted his questionnaire for the Senate Judiciary Committee. Here is the chronology Butler offers for his nomination:

On June 29, 2026, Senator Roger Wicker contacted me about a potential vacancy on the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. I spoke with Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith the following day. On July 1, 2026, an official from the White House Counsel's Office contacted me to arrange an interview. On July 13, 2026, I interviewed with officials from the White House Counsel's Office. Following my interview, I received periodic updates from Senator Wicker about the process. On October I, 2026, President Trump called to inform me that he planned to nominate me for a position on the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

There is a very relevant date missing here. On September 28, 2026, Judge Southwick publicly announced that he would take senior status. Yet three months earlier, Senator Wicker contacted Butler about the potential vacancy.

As I said from the outset, the fix was in. There was some sort of deal involving Wicker, Southwick, and the White House. I'm sure this interview was pro forma. and doubt any other candidates were interviewed. Judge Southwick could have announced his intentions at any time in August or early September, but he waited until the last possible moment to jam up the process, and ensure Butler would not go down. I do hope at least one Senator asks Butler if he is aware of any communications in which Judge Southwick, directly or indirectly, conditioned his willingness to take senior status if Butler is the nominee.

As for the rest of the SJQ, let's just say Butler's pantry is bare. Or, the Butler didn't do it.

Butler went to law school between 2005 and 2008, but he wasn't a member of the Federalist Society. That makes sense, as he wrote critically of Justice Scalia, originalism, and the Second Amendment. He wasn't a member while he clerked. Indeed, he didn't become a member of the Federalist Society until 2016. I suspect lots of people joined before or after Trump's victory. It would help with career prospects. He has never held any leadership positions in FedSoc. But rest assured that he was active in the Inn of Court and the Mississippi Bar, holding several leadership positions.

Butler has extensive experience in employment law. In addition to the publications I flagged, Butler speaks and writes often about the EEOC, FLSA, and related topics of municipal law. His only professional exposure to constitutional law involves defendant local officials who are sued for violating First Amendment rights. After Olivier v. City of Brandon, his most significant case was as defense counsel in a wrongful death case. He taught at the Mississippi College of Law "periodic[ally]" between 2008 and 2016 but does not recall which semesters he taught. He also does not have copies of the syllabi.

Here is how Butler describes his pro bono work:

Over the course of my career, I have accepted pro bono clients, typically through the Mission First Legal Aid Clinic or the Mississippi Volunteers Lawyers Project. I have assisted with adoptions, child visitation matters, and other domestic issues. I also have provided pro bono services to a local church, including contract review and procedure drafting, in connection with the operation of a faith-based children's center. I advised a local pastor on a land acquisition that he is considering using for a fellowship facility. And I have volunteered, along with others at my law firm, at Stewpot Community Services, where we served meals to people experiencing homelessness.

There is no pro bono work that would remotely be associated with the conservative legal movement. And no, working for a church does not necessarily make a person conservative.

If I were to show you this questionnaire, without any knowledge of Mississippi politics, would you possibly think this was a viable record for the Fifth Circuit? No.

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7728. Don’t Get Caught Off Guard by the First Frost Again — Bookmark This Checklist for Next Year

From HVAC systems to roofs and paint cans, these simple maintenance tasks can prevent big-ticket repairs.

In years past, when I’ve failed to prep my home for the first frost, I’ve ended up with burst garden hoses, broken tree limbs and cars that won’t start. But sometimes, procrastinating on winterizing a home can lead to even more severe problems, including foundation damage and burst pipes.

“If you want to save money and protect your pocket book, then jump on the winterization of your home and yard,” says home improvement expert Todd Tripp. “Before the first frost is also an excellent time to put your yard and equipment to sleep, so that it will start fresh for you in the spring.”

Ahead, Tripp and other experts walk through exactly what to do before the first frost of the season.

Water that accumulates around a home during winter can cause foundation damage as it freezes and thaws. Before the first frost comes, clean leaves and other debris from the gutters and downspouts, check for leaks and extend downspouts so they carry water at least 10 feet away from the house.

Common mistake: “Don’t clean the gutters too early in the fall, before nearby trees have finished shedding their leaves,” says remodeling expert Michael DiMartino.

Many outdoor water systems fall victim to the first freeze, bursting as the water inside of them expands into ice. To prevent this:

“It’s also a good idea to put the hoses and other garden equipment in a shed, so they’re covered and out of the elements,” says Tripp.

Freezing water can split plumbing pipes. Then, once temperatures rise, the water leaking out can cause significant damage. To prevent this, use foam insulation sleeves, insulation tape or heat tape around pipes that run through unheated areas, such as garages, crawls spaces, basements, attics and exterior walls.

“Also, look for gaps around windows, doors, foundations and where pipes enter the home, and seal them properly, since cold drafts can make vulnerable plumbing even more susceptible to freezing,” says plumber Tim Fancher. As a bonus, this will also help keep mice and spiders out.

Pro-tip: know where your main water shutoff is, says Fancher. If a pipe does burst, quickly shutting off the water will help mitigate damage.

Frost can cause weak trees limbs to fall, potentially damaging your roof or car, so trim trees before the winter season begins. That will also keep dead leaves from accumulating on your roof.

While you’re at it, prune shrubbery and cut back perennial plants. “Before the frost comes is also a good time to put in your winter fertilizer,” says Tripp. “Blend on your lawn and in your flowerbeds so that it will percolate down into the soil over the winter.”

Cracks or damaged seals can let in moisture, which will cause further damage, plus invite cold drafts. Before the first frost, caulk any gaps and fix damaged weather stripping. “This will also save you a lot of money on your heating bill, plus keep moisture and mold out of your house,” says Tripp.

Also, fogging between your window panes is often a sign that the window seal has failed, and the window may not be insulating your house as well as it once did, says DiMartino.

Any damage to your roof will likely get worse once temperatures drop. Before the first frost, visually inspect your roof for missing, loose or damaged shingles and signs of water intrusion. Also, check the attic for moisture.

Pro-tip: “If you notice moisture in the attic or leaks in the home’s living spaces, it could be a sign that the roof needs to be repaired or replaced,” says DiMartino.

A freezing evening is no time to have the furnace fail. That could lead to burst pipes and even jeopardize your family’s safety. Home improvement expert Eric Goranson recommends hiring a pro to inspect your system every year, plus tune it for maximum efficiency.

While you’re at it, don’t forget to winterize your air conditioning system. “It’s not completely necessary to cover the outside condenser unit, but it’s a good practice to cover it or wrap it to protect it from frost,” says Tripp.

Safety check: Before using your furnace or fireplace in the fall, check your chimney for debris like spiderwebs and bird nests, which could cause it to not vent properly, or even catch on fire.

Cold weather can reduce your battery’s cold cranking amps, making it hard to start on the first cold morning, says Goranson. Before the first frost, test your battery, check your tires and windshield wipers and bring other neglected maintenance up to date.

Pro-tip: Run a Top Tier fuel through your vehicle at least once a month. “Those have cleaners in them that help keep your engine’s fuel system clean,” says Goranson.

Drain fuel or put fuel stabilizers in gas-powered lawnmowers, trimmers and blowers, before stowing them in the shed. “The best trick I was ever told, which has worked for over 30 years, is to drain the fuel out of your landscape equipment, then start it up and let it run until it’s completely out of gas,” says Tripp. “That gets all the fuel out of your carburetor so that it does not varnish or gum up, and it will start in the spring every time.”

For electric-powered equipment, charge the batteries to the manufacturer-recommended levels, then leave them in a temperature-controlled space.

If your garage isn’t insulated, chances are there are items in there that won’t fare well when temperatures drop. Especially check the storage instructions on paints and other liquids, plus battery-powered equipment. Also, don’t forget to check the seals on your garage door.

Pro-tip: Move shovels and ice melt to a place where they’re easy to access, leave a clear walking path through the garage and designate somewhere to put wet boots and tools, says garage expert Alan Bernau Jr. “You want to be able to use the garage in winter, not just cram everything into it,” he says.

#7727. Op-Ed: Crime Drops—Locally Collected Data Drives National Headlines

A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Share on X X.com Share on Facebook Facebook Email Email

This opinion piece by CJIS Special Agent in Charge Timothy A. Ferguson was published by the Bridgeport News on October 19, 2026.

Across the country, you saw the headlines. Violent crime declined historically last year—dropping an estimated 9.3% from 2024 to 2025. Murder and nonnegligent manslaughter estimated offenses saw an even larger dip of 18.1%.

In West Virginia, crime was also trending downward.

These headlines are based on data reported to the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program by more than 17,000 agencies, covering 96.2% of the U.S. population. It is the responsibility of the FBI’s UCR Program, located within the Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) Division, in Clarksburg, West Virginia, to collect and publish the data from all 50 states to provide a national picture of reported crime.

This is no small feat. Every day, states and agencies translate local and state crime categories into the national standard and submit their data to the FBI. The UCR Program publishes this data monthly on the Crime Data Explorer to promote transparency and allow you to view timely crime data.

The program also uses the data to develop special reports on topics that matter to you — such as crime in schools, aggravated assault with a firearm, and teen/domestic violence. Then once a year, the program sorts through more than 700 million data points to present you the annual snapshot of crime.

Data collection is just a small fraction of what is accomplished at the CJIS Division. Other efforts also make headlines or prevent you from seeing a tragedy on the news.

Tips actioned by the National Threat Operations Center (NTOC) stop school shootings and help with investigations. Super intelligence capabilities incorporated into NTOC enhance the speed and precision of tip triage, strengthening our ability to process the highest priority tips first so we can promptly share critical threat information with federal, state, and local law enforcement.

Criminal history information from the Interstate Identification Index prevents criminals from becoming your child’s teacher or bus driver. Wants and warrants within the National Crime Information Center help police arrest violent criminals.

Detectives can identify subjects and victims through fingerprints submitted to the Next Generation Identification System.

The division’s mission is to provide our partners with the criminal justice information they need while preserving civil liberties. Sharing that information with officers on the frontlines results in arrests that take criminals off the street and keep neighborhoods safe.

It helps law enforcement return to their families at the end of their shifts. It crushes violent crime and defends the homeland.

When you see headlines of declining crime, know the work to determine that, and the investigations that preceded it, are touched by your neighbors dedicated to the mission at the FBI’s CJIS Division.

Timothy A. Ferguson is assistant director in charge of the FBI’s Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) Division in Clarksburg, West Virginia. CJIS provides vital systems and services to local, state, tribal, and federal agencies that help ensure public safety. These include the National Crime Information Center; the FBI’s Next Generation Identification System and associated biometric services; the National Instant Criminal Background Check System for firearm purchases; the National Threat Operations Center, which receives and processes tips from the public; and the Uniform Crime Reporting Program, which publishes crime and law enforcement statistical data.

#7726. If You Spot OTR on a Truck, Here’s What It Means

Those three letters on a semi-truck usually refer to long-distance driving. Learn what OTR means and how different trucking routes work.

Trucks are full of weird and useful features that most people overlook without knowing their real purpose. Some have long spikes on their wheels. Others might feature amber lights on top. You might even see diamond shaped signs. But what about OTR written on a truck?

What can look like a government code can have a specific meaning in the trucking industry. Learn what OTR means, how long-haul work compares with shorter routes, and why the context matters.

In trucking, OTR stands for “over-the-road.” It refers to long-haul trucking, where drivers transport freight across long distances, often through several states or into Canada. According to trucking company Schneider, OTR drivers can spend weeks away from home. Many drive trucks with sleeper cabs that provide a place to rest between shifts.

OTR describes the type of work, not a specific truck. It’s also not a required marking. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) requires certain identifying information, including a company’s name and USDOT number, on interstate commercial trucks, but OTR isn’t part of that requirement.

The letters can also mean something different depending on where they appear. In the tire industry, OTR stands for “off-the-road,” referring to heavy-duty tires used on construction and mining equipment. OTR Diagnostics is also the name of a maintenance tool that helps truck owners check engine problems and other vehicle information.

OTR truck drivers transport freight over long distances, often making several stops along the way. Their jobs can also involve inspecting their trucks, handling delivery paperwork, and sometimes helping load or unload cargo.

Because these trips can last for weeks, drivers often sleep in their trucks or stop at other places along their routes. The FMCSA limits how long commercial drivers can drive without taking required breaks and rest periods.

Drivers who operate most full-size tractor-trailers need a Class A commercial driver’s license (CDL). Depending on the company and route, drivers may spend several weeks working before returning home.

OTR drivers cover the longest distances and may spend weeks away from home. Regional drivers work within a particular area of the country, often returning home weekly or more frequently. Local drivers generally stay closer to home and return after each shift, although they can still work long hours.

There’s also dedicated trucking, where drivers regularly transport freight for the same customer or between the same locations. These routes can be local, regional, or long-distance, depending on the company.

The exact distances and schedules vary between employers, so the terms don’t always describe the same mileage or amount of time away from home.

#7725. S. Ct. Suspends District Court's Injunction Blocking Border Barrier Building

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"There is no such thing as a 'constitutional' major-questions claim."

From today's Supreme Court unsigned opinion in Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church (with Justice Jackson essentially dissenting):

Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) grants the Secretary of Homeland Security broad authority to construct border barriers and roads "to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States." The same section expressly authorizes the Secretary "'to waive all legal requirements'" as "'necessary to ensure expeditious construction'" of those barriers and roads, and sharply limits judicial review of all claims arising from such waiver determinations. Specifically, the statute provides that "'[a] cause of action or claim may only be brought alleging a violation of the Constitution of the United States'" and courts "'shall not have jurisdiction'" over nonconstitutional claims. §102(c)(2)(A).

Earlier this year, the Secretary invoked Section 102's waiver authority to initiate a border-construction project at the U.S.–Mexico border, in a region that U.S. Customs and Border Protection has designated the "Big Bend Sector." The Secretary found that the Big Bend Sector "is an area of high illegal entry" requiring additional border barriers, and waived the application of a variety of environmental and conservation laws to facilitate expeditious construction.

Shortly thereafter, respondents—an individual river guide, an environmental nonprofit, and a nonprofit organization dedicated to preserving a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas—challenged those waiver determinations by filing suit in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas. Respondents claimed, among other things, that the Secretary's waiver determinations "violat[ed] the major questions doctrine under the U.S. Constitution, Article I, Section 1." Although styled as constitutional, that claim simply alleged that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority in issuing the waivers.

On October 2, 2026, the District Court entered a preliminary injunction blocking the Secretary's waivers and halting all associated construction. The District Court acknowledged that its jurisdiction was limited to constitutional claims. But it nonetheless concluded that respondents' "major questions doctrine claim" qualified because, in its view, the "major questions doctrine is a constitutional clear statement rule grounded in separation of powers." The court further held that respondents' "major questions doctrine claim" was likely to succeed on the merits because the Secretary lacked "'clear congressional authorization' to issue" the waivers. Because the Fifth Circuit lacks jurisdiction to hear this case, IIRIRA §102(c)(2)(C), the Solicitor General filed an application requesting either summary reversal or a stay of the District Court's preliminary injunction.

We grant the requested stay. The Government is exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument that the District Court lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate respondents' so-called major-questions-doctrine claim. However it is labeled, respondents' claim does not "'alleg[e] a violation of the Constitution of the United States,'" the only type of claim the statute permits district courts to adjudicate. IIRIRA §102(c)(2)(A). It alleges instead that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority. And we have long recognized that "claims simply alleging" that the Executive Branch has exceeded its "statutory authority are not 'constitutional' claims." Dalton v. Specter (1994).

That conclusion does not change where, as here, a plaintiff invokes the major-questions doctrine. Many canons and rules of statutory interpretation reflect constitutional principles, including "constitutional avoidance, the clear-statement federalism rules, and the presumption against retroactivity." When courts invoke those canons, however, they do so in service of adjudicating statutory claims, not constitutional ones. The same is true when a court invokes "the major questions canon of statutory interpretation." There is no such thing as a "constitutional" major-questions claim….

Respondents claim that construction in the Big Bend Sector will diminish their ability to use and enjoy the area. But Congress's enactment of IIRIRA §102(c)—which permits the Secretary to waive the requirements of environmental-protection and other conservation laws—reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert. And courts "of equity cannot, in their discretion, reject the balance that Congress has struck in a statute." The Government's interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents….

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7724. Is a Reverse Osmosis Filter System Actually Worth It? We Break Down Every Cost

What’s lurking in your water? RO filters get rid of everything from microplastics to heavy metals, but are they overkill?

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

In this installment of Home 2.0, we dive into reverse osmosis filtration for the kitchen, its benefits and hidden costs — plus which households should invest in the technology, and who can skip it.

I’ve lived in some places with questionable drinking water. One town issued a notice that the municipal water supply had experienced a sewage incident. Another had an arsenic problem. I’ve also lived on well water, with concerns of contamination from nearby agricultural fields.

My solution used to be buying five-gallon jugs of spring water. But that was costly and a hassle, so six years ago, I switched to an under-sink reverse osmosis (RO) filter for my drinking and cooking water.

Under-sink RO filters work like this: water passes through a series of filters, including an RO membrane, which removes dissolved substances — including lead, arsenic, nitrates, forever chemicals, chlorine, fluoride and sediment — down to 0.0001 microns. The cleaned water then comes out through a faucet, installed near the sink.

“Reverse osmosis provides the safest level of drinking water possible,” says international water filtration specialist Andrew D. Daily. “It strips out 100% of bacteria, cysts, dissolved solids, chlorine, rust, viruses and microplastics.”

But RO systems are also a considerable investment. So, we asked a range of health and plumbing experts for their thoughts on who should get an RO system, plus how to pick the right one. Ahead is what they said, how much RO systems cost up front and over time, and whether it’s worth the upgrade.

RO water systems range from a few hundred dollars to over $1,000. The good news is that if you have basic plumbing knowledge and are comfortable drilling a hole in your countertop, installing one can be a DIY task. Otherwise, pro installation usually runs upwards of $300, not including add-ons like a refrigerator/ice-maker connection, leak protection, an additional electric outlet and other plumbing modifications.

The biggest downside to RO systems is that they waste water. For every gallon that comes out of the faucet, somewhere between one-half and four gallons get flushed down the drain through the filtration process. That means if you use 5 gallons of water a day for cooking and drinking, the RO system wastes between 2.5 and 20 gallons.

Over a year, that adds up to between 500 and 8,500 gallons, depending on your RO system. On the low end, that’s only a few pennies more on your yearly water utility bill, but on the high end, it could be close to $100.

Some RO water systems also require electricity. The amount of power they consume varies by model, but usually falls between 20 and 40 watts per hour. Since RO systems typically run for less than an hour a day, even if you live in a place with high electricity rates, they should add only a few dollars a year to your electricity bill.

Maintaining RO systems is an easy DIY task, though some people choose to pay a pro to keep track of it for them. Expect to spend roughly the following for DIY maintenance:

Daily recommends buying only name-brand filters, even though they’re more expensive. “Name brands follow strict regulations,” he says. ”Generic China-based deals often do not provide the same protection.”

A quality RO system can last 10 years or longer with proper maintenance. “Many parts, including filters, membranes, faucets and tanks can be replaced individually,” says plumbing expert Danielle Smith. “Once a system gets older, though, replacement may make more sense than repeated repairs.”

“The biggest thing for me is convenience,” says environmental and wellness expert Helen Christoni, who has an AquaTru system. “We use water all day long, drinking it, cooking with it and filling water bottles. Once installed, it just became part of my kitchen and my family’s daily health.”

Herman Hartanto, founder of Tampa Fast Home Buyer, has a Waterdrop G3P600 in his kitchen ($429 retail). It’s a tankless model, a feature he appreciates since it takes up minimal cabinet space. He also likes the display with real-time reports on total dissolved solids (TDS) and filter health. His only complaint is the occasional noise it generates. “The pump that draws the water on demand makes quite loud noise, which I can feel clearly at night when everything is silent,” he says.

Personally, I’ve used two RO filter systems. My first one was an iSpring, which I chose because of its affordability. It worked well, but like Hartanto, I found the pump noisy (even though mine had a water-holding tank). My second one, which I’ve only recently installed, is a Waterdrop X12 Pro, which I chose to upgrade to because of its water-saving efficiency, ability to add calcium and magnesium back into the water, clear display and range of other premium features. So far, I’ve found it to be quiet, efficient, and free of quirks (though at $1,400 off-sale, the price is a bit of a shocker).

Depending on what type of contaminants you have in your water, there are several alternatives to an under-sink RO water filter:

“Find out what’s in your water before buying anything,” says Smith. “Don’t choose a system based only on how many stages it has or how many contaminants the box says it removes. Instead, start with your water and choose the system around what you actually need.”

If you’re worried about contaminants like microplastics, arsenic, lead, forever chemicals, pesticides and pharmaceuticals, then an RO filter is a good choice.

“Water quality can vary tremendously depending on where you live, and even your home’s plumbing can affect what ultimately comes out of your faucet,” says Christoni. “Reverse osmosis addresses such a broad range of contaminants, and with an under-sink system, that purified water is available all day long without having to think about it.”

For Daily, the biggest reason to invest in a RO system is microplastics. “The amount of microplastics found in human brains, blood and organs have been increasing yearly,” he says. “Although there is not enough information to prove a detrimental effect on our health, many of my clients choose a cautious approach to water treatment.”

Otherwise, Daily says that RO filters are overkill in most U.S. cities, where tap water is generally considered safe. Even in Mexico, where water is often contaminated, he usually recommends sticking with under-sink ultrafiltration systems, since they’re a fraction of the cost, don’t waste water and don’t require power or space for a reservoir.

If you’re currently buying bottled water, then yes, an RO system will soon pay for itself. But, otherwise, it really just depends on what you want to remove from your water. If you have arsenic, nitrates, salts, microplastics, fluoride, sulfates and other dissolved solids (TDS), RO systems are a great solution.

Otherwise, a less-expensive ultrafiltration system might be a better choice. Either way, having an under-sink filtration system is a good way to ensure your family has access to clean water, both on a daily basis and after flooding events and other natural disasters that contaminate city and well water.

#7723. Step Up Your Game With a DIY Folding Step Stool

This weekend project walks you through every cut and joint to make a foldable step stool you’ll actually use every day.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Turn leftover hardwood scraps into a rock-solid folding step stool that puts wobbly plastic versions to shame.

At some point in our lives we will need a folding step stool. You know, the one that stays out of the way but, gives you that little extra boost when you don’t need a full step ladder. In my case, I find myself reaching for a step stool more often than I’d like to admit especially when trying to reach into a work truck. When I need something, I prefer to make it and am happy to share the steps with you. Just because it is small doesn’t mean it isn’t as satisfying to make – enjoy!

On the miter saw and/or table saw, cut the top step (A), all four legs (B), the guides (C), ad the bottom crossbrace (E). Set aside everything but the legs (B) until later.

Using a compass with a pencil, draw 1-1/2-inch diameter half-circles at the bottom of each leg (B) to match the 1/2-inch width of the leg.

Use a disc or belt sander with a coarse-grit sandpaper (80 or 100-grit) to shape the ends of the legs by sanding up to the marked pencil lines for your arch. Once you have sanded to the line, work your way up to 220-grit sandpaper for a smoother finish.

Using a router table or a router equipped with a 1/4-inch round-over bit, round over all the edges of the step (A) and all four legs (B). Be sure to use clamps to hold the pieces while making your passes with the router.

With all the parts machined, sand all the components to 220 grit and apply a couple of coats of a wood finish of your choice. Allow the finish to dry before moving on to assembly.

Spread wood glue in hole 3 at the top of each inside leg (B). Insert the ends of the 3/4-in. dowel cross brace (D) and tap the legs on with a rubber mallet until D is fully seated.

Set the 1-1/4-in.-square cross brace (E) between the bottoms of the legs, with its bottom edge 2-1/8 in. up from the bottom of the legs. To keep the legs parallel while you drill, clamp a scrap the same length as the cross brace (E) between them at mid-height. Check for square.

Using hole 4 in each leg as a guide, drill a 1/2-in. hole about 1 in. deep into the center of each end of the cross brace (E). Glue 1/2-in. dowels, cut longer than the holes are deep, and drive them through the legs with a mallet until they bottom out in the cross brace (E).

Lock each of the four joints with a single brad nail through the leg into the dowel. Trim the protruding ends of all the dowels flush with a pull saw.

Flip the top step (A) upside down. Position the guide rails (C) 1/2-in. in from each side and centered front to back, leaving 1-1/2-in. at the front and back. Trace around each rail.

Drill two 1/4-in. holes, 3/4-in. deep, centered on each outline. Keep the bit plumb when drilling (or drill at the drill press).

Insert dowel centers in the holes. Align each rail with its outline and press down to mark the hole locations. Drill matching 1/4-in. holes in the rails, about 7/8-in. deep. That’s slightly deeper than the dowel needs, which leaves room for glue.

Glue and insert 1/4-in x 1-1/2-in. dowels and secure the guide rails (C) to the step (A).

Thread 1/4-inch x 3-1/2-inch carriage bolts through hole 1 in the center of the legs to connect an outside leg to the outside of each of the connected inside legs. Put a washer between each pair of legs and secure with a nylon lock nut on the inside of the inside legs.

Connect the two outside legs (B) to the sides of the guide rails (C) by threading 1/4-inch x 2-1/2-inch pan head screws through hole 5 in the guide rails and through hole 2 on the outside legs. Use a washer on the outside of the guide rails and pliers to hold the nylon lock nuts while you tighten them into the 5/8-inch countersunk holes.

The strap acts as a stop, limiting how far the legs can open. Wrap one end of an upholstery strap around the middle of the top cross brace (D) and staple it in place with a narrow-crown stapler. Open the stool until the seat sits level, then pull the strap snug and staple the other end centered on the underside of the top step (A). Use several 1/2-in. staples at each end so the strap holds securely.

A step stool should be about 11 to 16-in. wide to fit both feet comfortably side by side. For a portable or compact version, stay toward the narrow end of that range.

A single-step stool should be 6 to 9-in. tall. That’s a good height for reaching into a truck bed, helping kids reach a tall bathroom sink, or getting to the top pantry shelves.

Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, of Ontario, Canada, was sentenced today to 50 years in prison for offenses related to a 2020 attack on correctional officers at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood. This sentence will run consecutive to the 40-year sentence he is currently serving for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS.

“Bahnasawy, who is already serving a 40-year sentence in federal prison for plotting mass casualty attacks in New York City on behalf of ISIS, savagely attacked corrections officers once again on behalf of ISIS,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time.”

Miller for the Middle District of Pennsylvania. “Today’s sentence reflects our unwavering commitment to fight those who perpetrate violence in the name of ISIS even behind prison walls.”

“Although he was behind bars, this convicted terrorist committed a horrific attack on two corrections officers in the name of ISIS, which they fortunately survived,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “Today’s sentencing shows that violent attacks by those who support the evil ideology of ISIS or other foreign terrorist organizations cannot be tolerated by our society. Fighting terrorism is a central part of the FBI’s mission to protect the American people, and the FBI is committed to working with our law enforcement partners to hold these vicious criminals accountable.”

Bahnasawy was an inmate at USP Allenwood who, on Dec. 7, 2020, attacked two corrections officers using a weapon made from part of a steel desk in his cell. Bahnasawy stabbed one officer in the head and face, and, when a second responded to assist, Bahnasawy stabbed her in the hand.

The first officer eventually lost his right eye as a result of the attack. When Bahnasawy was restrained, a note was found in his sock that read, “This is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State.” A pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) was also found taped to the inside of a locker door in Bahnasawy’s prison cell. Bahnasawy pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to ISIS, a designated foreign terrorist organization.

At the time of the attacks at USP Allenwood, Bahnasawy was serving a 40-year sentence for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS. Bahnasawy, a then-20-year-old Canadian citizen and resident, plotted with Talha Haroon and Russell Salic to conduct bombings and shootings in heavily populated areas of New York City during the Islamic holy month of Ramadhan in 2016, all in the name of ISIS.

An undercover FBI agent (UC) infiltrated the co-conspirators’ terrorist plot, posing as an ISIS supporter prepared to join in the attacks. The FBI arrested Bahnasawy in May 2016 after he traveled from Canada to the New York City area in preparation for the attacks, and he has been in custody since that time.

This case was investigated by the FBI’s Philadelphia Field Office.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Geoffrey MacArthur for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and Deputy Chief Larry Schneider of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section prosecuted the case.

#7721. Andrew McCarthy on the Hegseth Impeachment

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

A prominent conservative legal commentator explains why Hegseth should be convicted on at least some of the charges.

Yesterday, I wrote about why Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth deserves to be impeached and convicted for his role in in starting an unconstitutional war and perpetrating over 200 cases of outright murder with the "drug boat" strikes. Today GOP Rep. Thomas Massie filed impeachment charges in the House of Representatives. Even if they don't pass in the narrowly Republican-controlled lame duck Congress, they will almost certainly do so in the incoming Democratic one. Meanwhile prominent conservative legal commentator, national security law expert and former federal prosecutor Andrew McCarthy has published an excellent overview of the charges in the National Review.

McCarthy is far to my right, and far more sympathetic to the War on Drugs (I myself believe it should be abolished). Thus, it's notable that he and I agree that Hegseth should be convicted for his role in the drug boat strikes, which McCarthy characterizes as "indefensible":

I do not believe there is any viable justification for the extrajudicial killings by military force of operators of suspected drug boats. Drug trafficking is a crime, not an act of war. Our law addresses it through trial and imprisonment, not the use of military force…. The administration has not proved that the boats were ferrying narcotics, much less that the drugs were headed to the United States. The president's designation of Venezuelan criminal gangs as foreign terrorist organizations, besides being legally dubious (drug dealing is not "terrorist activity" as defined in federal law), does not authorize the use of force (it instead makes material support to the organization a crime and helps the government cut off funding sources). While the unauthorized killings in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific have not drawn the level of public ire that the Iran war has, they are indefensible, and Hegseth has been their loudest, crudest champion.

As noted in my earlier post, this view is similar to that of John Yoo, well-known former Bush Administration official and leading conservative advocate of sweeping executive power over national security and foreign affairs.

McCarthy also argues Hegseth should be convicted on at least one other charge:

Similarly, I do not believe there is any defending Hegseth on the charge that he has abused command authority and violated constitutional separation-of-powers principles in trying to discipline and censure Senator Kelly, a retired Navy captain (who remains subject to the Uniform Code of Military Justice). Hegseth's actions, undoubtedly endorsed by the president, constituted unlawful command influence. More importantly, they abused executive power in an effort to muffle congressional criticism. The haughty Hegseth was playing a dangerous game here; if it has now come back to bite him, he has himself to blame.

This charge is less within my expertise than some of the others. But I agree with McCarthy here.

McCarthy also appears to recognize that the Iran War is illegal, but suggests that Hegseth does not deserve impeachment on this score, because he was just obeying Trump's orders and implementing his policy. He also notes (correctly) that previous presidents have gotten away with similar initiations of war without congressional authorization.

I disagree for reasons summarized in my previous post:

Obviously, the ultimate perpetrator of these illegal acts is not Hegseth, but Trump. The former was following the latter's illegal orders (though he likely also helped influence Trump to give those orders in the first place). But sanctioning officials for obeying illegal orders is still important. That's one of the lessons of the Nuremberg trials.

I would add that Hegseth wasn't just some low-level flunky merely obeying orders. He has had a major influence on policy, and was one of the key architects of both the Iran War and the boat strikes. OK, maybe he is a flunky; but not a low-level one. He bears far greater responsibility than, e.g., servicemembers at the bottom of the chain of command.

As also noted in my earlier post, it is indeed true that previous presidents, such as Barack Obama, have gotten away with starting illegal wars. Obama deserved to be impeached, as well. But that makes it all the more imperative to start enforcing this part of the Constitution more effectively. Moreover, the Iran War is much larger and has had far worse effects than any other illegal wars of the last several decades. Obama's illegal wars were much smaller, by comparison.

I will not say much about McCarthy's analysis of the other charges, except briefly on that focused on the removal of Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro. McCarthy laments that Trump left the brutal socialist regime in power (minus Maduro), but suggests that the intervention might have been legally justified by the precedent of the 1989 US military action that removed and captured Panamanian strongman Manuel Noriega. I differ for reasons I outlined here:

Defenders of the legality of Trump's actions cite the 1989 invasion of Panama, which was undertaken in large part for the purpose of apprehending Panamian dictator Manuel Noriega; like Maduro, Noriega was charged with smuggling illegal drugs into the US. But the 1989 Panama precedent does not actually justify Trump's actions. On December 15, 1989 (five days before the US invasion), Noriega foolishly announced that Panama and the US were in a "state of war," thereby creating conflict between the two countries that did not exist in the Venezuela case. In addition, Panamanian forces had killed or wounded two US military personnel in the Panama Canal area, and detained other American citizens. Unlike Noriega in 1989, the Venezuelan regime did not declare war on the US or otherwise initiate a military conflict. Thus, congressional authorization is needed to make any US military intervention constitutional.

That said, I think the Maduro intervention charge is much weaker than the Iran War and boat strike charges. The Maduro action was on a much smaller scale, and has not had anything like the same horrific effects. The abusive prosecution charge is also more compelling than that focused on Maduro. Congress would do well to focus attention on the strongest charges and convict Hegseth on them.

#7720. What Is “Heart Attack Snow,” and Why Is It So Dangerous?

Heavy, wet snow can turn an ordinary winter chore into a health risk. Learn why people call it heart attack snow and how to shovel safely.

Shoveling snow can be a dangerous winter chore. Icy walkways can cause serious falls, and prolonged exposure to the cold can lead to hypothermia or frostbite. Another safety concern is something called “heart attack snow.”

The name sounds dramatic, but it points to a real concern for people clearing sidewalks and driveways in winter. For those in snowy climates, understanding the risks of heart attack snow is important before picking up a shovel.

Understanding the risks can help prevent a routine chore from becoming a medical emergency.

Heart attack snow is a nickname for heavy, wet snow that’s harder to shovel than dry, powdery snow. The name comes from the strain that lifting this type of snow can place on the heart. According to the National Weather Service, snow with a higher water content weighs more, making each shovelful harder to lift.

The added effort can quickly raise heart rate and blood pressure. Cold temperatures also cause blood vessels to narrow, making the heart work harder. The American Heart Association warns that this combination can trigger a heart attack or sudden cardiac arrest.

The association says the risks are especially concerning for “people who already have cardiovascular risks like a sedentary lifestyle or obesity,” including those with a history of smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, or high blood pressure. People who have previously suffered a heart attack or stroke also face greater risks.

Even lighter, powdery snow can be dangerous, especially when large amounts require repeated lifting or hours of clearing.

Before heading outside, people should warm up indoors and stretch gently. Dressing in layers helps protect against the cold, while staying hydrated is important even when someone doesn’t feel thirsty.

The American Heart Association recommends pushing snow rather than lifting it whenever possible. When lifting is necessary, smaller loads and frequent breaks can help limit physical strain. A snow blower can also reduce the amount of lifting, although operating one still requires effort.

Slippery surfaces are another concern. “Walking on ice is extremely dangerous,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The agency recommends using rock salt or another de-icing product to keep walkways clear of ice. Sand can also help prevent slipping.

People with heart disease or significant cardiovascular risk factors should have someone else handle snow removal, according to the American Heart Association.

Recognizing the warning signs of a heart attack is equally important. Chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, dizziness, nausea, cold sweats, or discomfort in the arms, back, or jaw can all signal a serious problem. Symptoms aren’t always severe and can vary from person to person.

Anyone experiencing possible heart attack symptoms should stop shoveling immediately and call 911. The American Heart Association advises against waiting to see whether symptoms go away.

American Heart Association, “Snow Shoveling, Cold Temperatures Combine for Perfect Storm of Heart Health Hazards” American Heart Association, “Warning Signs of a Heart Attack” National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Preparedness” Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, “Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm”

#7718. Yes, Different Curb Colors Have a Meaning — A Guide to Decoding Them

A painted curb can tell drivers where to park, stop, or unload. Here's what red, yellow, green, blue, and white curbs usually mean.

Finding a parking spot isn’t always as simple as pulling up to an empty space. Sometimes different curb colors come with their own parking rules, and drivers might not know what those colors mean. The different curb colors help drivers know where they can park, stop, or drop someone off.

The California Driver’s Handbook lists five common colors: red, white, yellow, green, and blue. But those colors don’t mean exactly the same thing everywhere. Cities have their own parking rules, and some areas have restrictions that only apply during certain hours. Los Angeles, for example, has different rules for loading zones, while Seattle uses yellow paint to mark some areas near driveways that drivers need to keep clear.

Learn what the five colors generally mean and what drivers should know before parking.

Red curbs generally mean drivers can’t stop or park there, even for a few minutes. That includes waiting in the car while someone runs into a store. They’re common near fire hydrants, intersections, and bus stops, where parked cars could block traffic or get in the way. Some red zones still allow buses to stop to pick up or drop off passengers.

White curbs usually allow drivers to stop long enough to pick up or drop off passengers. They’re often found outside hotels, schools, and hospitals.

But they aren’t regular parking spaces. Drivers generally need to stay with their vehicles and leave once their passengers get in or out. Some cities have different rules, though. San Francisco, for example, also allows certain white curbs to be used for quickly loading or unloading goods.

Yellow curbs usually mark loading zones. They’re often found near businesses where delivery drivers need somewhere to stop while dropping off packages or other goods. Commercial vehicles can typically use these areas for a short time, although some cities allow passenger vehicles to stop there, too. These aren’t regular parking spaces, and nearby signs usually explain how long drivers can stop.

Green curbs generally mean drivers can park, but only for a short time. They’re common near businesses where customers might need to stop for a few minutes. The time limit isn’t always the same, so drivers should check the curb or nearby signs before leaving their cars. Some spaces also have parking meters or restrictions during certain hours.

Blue curbs mark parking spaces for people with disabilities. Cities often place these spaces near building entrances to make them easier to access. Drivers need a valid disability parking placard or qualifying license plate to park in these spaces. Without one, they can’t use the spot, even for a quick stop.

The striped areas next to accessible parking spaces also need to stay clear so people have enough room to get in and out of their vehicles.

#7716. 13 Potted Plants You Can—and Should—Winter Indoors

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 9, 2026 5:31 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Plenty of gardeners place their houseplants outdoors for the summer and enjoy them indoors the rest of the year. So why not try a similar strategy, and save a little money while you’re at it, by bringing your favorite cold-tender plants inside when the temperature drops so they’ll be ready to grow again when spring and summer rolls around?

Before you bring your outdoor plants in for the winter, you’ll need to do a bit of preparation. Start by inspecting them for pests and treating, if necessary. Repot if a plant needs it, and cut down on (or eliminate) fertilizing. Some plants can simply be brought indoors as houseplants, others should be forced into dormancy for a few months of cool storage, and still others are best kept going by making rooted cuttings. The following are a few cold-tender plants that you can bring inside each winter and then continue to enjoy outside for many summers to come.

While some palm trees are hardy in the winters of the Deep South, most palms need help to survive winter temperatures, even only to 55 to 60 degrees Fahrenheit . It’s possible to cover and winterize some palms planted in the ground, but potted palms should come indoors (preferably to a bright, humid spot). Move palms to an indoor location that gets lots of light. Water them regularly to keep the soil moist until spring, and carry them back outdoors after nights warm back up to at least 50 or 60 degrees.

Leave cacti outdoors as late into the season as possible so that the combination of shorter days and cooler nights will stimulate a dormancy response. You’ll need to keep an eye on the thermometer and know the low-temperature threshold for your particular type of cactus. Some species may be able to withstand 20-degree temperatures, but others cannot. If unsure, move potted cacti indoors as soon as cold drops to about 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

Stop watering cacti 3 to 4 weeks before the move so the plants are dry, and check them carefully for pets like mealy bugs or mites. In general, cacti do best in a cool location with minimal water, as they go dormant. Transition them back outside in early spring, gradually introducing sunlight if the plants show any sign of burning.

Citrus trees can actively grow and flower in winter, and may also ripen fruit if they’re pollinated. Even without winter growth, it’s a good idea protect these plants during the chilly months. As the days get shorter, move potted citrus trees (typically, dwarf varieties of lime and lemon trees) to an interim space outdoors that gets some protection from the elements, like a porch with radiant heat, and cut back on watering.

Before the first frost, move the citrus tree into a brightly lit indoor room, ideally between 55 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit. Citrus plants are sensitive to the drying effects of air, so it’s best to position them away from heat vents and cold drafts. Provide supplemental humidity with a pebble tray or regular misting.

Move tropical hibiscus plants indoors when overnight temperatures reach the low 50s. Place them in a brightly lit room, and treat them like regular houseplants. Cut back on watering and fertilizing during these cooler months. Try to avoid heat vents and cold drafts, and put the plants on a pebble tray to boost the ambient humidity, if necessary. Prune tropical hibiscus three times during late fall and winter (October, December, and February) to maintain the plant’s shape.

Prune jasmine vines by at least 25 percent before bringing them in for winter, letting them adjust gradually by bringing them inside at night and slowly lengthening the time spent indoors. Some or all of the plant’s leaves will fall off, but new ones will grow again in time. Bring jasmine into a sunny room before frosty weather arrives, and keep it away from drying air vents and drafts. Use a pebble tray to boost humidity to about 30 percent.

Coleus plants are grown for their stunning foliage and adaptability to shade. The plants are annuals in most regions, though, since they do not like temperatures below 50 degrees Fahrenheit and cannot survive temperatures below freezing. Bring the potted plant indoors once nights hover near 50 degrees. Repot the plant if it is outgrowing its container.

Another option is to propagate coleus stems to use next spring. Cut a 6-inch healthy stem, remove low leaves, and dip the stem in a rooting hormone before planting it in a container with moist potting mix. Cover the container with a plastic bag for a few weeks and keep it in a warm and sunny spot; water regularly.

Aromatic rosemary is a favorite cooking herb for many fall and winter dishes. However, the plant does not always survive winters in USDA Zones 6 or lower. Start by planting a rosemary in a well-draining container. Bring potted rosemary indoors before the first freeze. Keep it in a cool location with fairly high humidity, but avoid overwatering; if its roots stay damp and cool, it can develop root rot.

Feel free to harvest from the plant, but never cut off more than about 20 percent of the foliage and avoid cutting into woody main stems. You also can propagate rosemary indoors at the end of the season with 4- to 6-inch cuttings from a stem with no flowers.

Elephant ears, or taro, is a tropical plant that can survive a light frost only; a true freeze will kill the tuber. Simply move potted elephant ears indoors to a cool bright location. For those grown in the ground, carefully dig up the elephant ear tuber when cool weather approaches and the foliage dies back (they won’t survive winter outdoors in USDA Zone 6 and lower). Cut stems down to about 4 to 6 inches, and gently wipe off excess dirt.

Place the tuber in a warm, dark location with good air circulation to dry out for a few days. Wrap the bulbs in paper or drop them in a paper bag and store them in a cool, dry, dark place. Check them periodically for rot (throw rotten ones away) and insect damage (treat with an insecticide). Beware that nearly all its parts are toxic to pets and people if ingested—we don’t recommend bringing it indoors if you have young children.

It is technically possible to bring Boston ferns indoors and overwinter them in their active state, but it gets very messy very quickly. Instead, let them rest. Put them in a cool, moderately light to dark location that will not freeze, like an unheated basement or garage.

Before bringing your fern inside, hose it down on a warm (60-degree Fahrenheit) day to spray away insects and loose leaves. Give it a light trim, and shake and ruffle the fronds to drop debris before carrying the plant to its indoor spot. Moisten dry soil as needed until spring. Don’t be alarmed if some leaves pale or drop.

Geranium is another plant that likes to sleep the winter away. Dig the plants out of the ground before the first freeze, and gently knock the soil off the roots. Allow the plants to dry in a cool, shady location for a couple of days. Place the plants upside down in a paper bag and close the top. Store them in a cool, dark location that stays between 55 and 60 degrees.

About 2 months before the last frost date, trim the stored geraniums and plant them in moist potting soil with two leaf nodes below the soil line. You also can propagate cuttings or bring potted geraniums indoors to a sunny window.

Thyme is a flavorful and aromatic perennial herb, but a tender one in regions 5 or lower. Plant culinary thyme in a container in spring, keeping it in a sunny, bright location with well-draining soil. Bring it indoors for winter before the first frost. If the herb’s roots are peeking though the bottom of the pot or it looks crowded, repot the thyme when you bring it in. It also can be divided easily.

Be sure to place the container near a sunny window with a western or southern exposure in a room that maintains a 60- to 70-degrees Fahrenheit temperature for most of the day. Prune or pinch off flowers to preserve the herb’s flavor. Water as needed, allowing the container dry out between watering. You can fertilize every week or two with a diluted solution of fish emulsion or liquid seaweed. Harvest sprigs as needed for winter dishes.

Although Musa basjoo, Musella lasiocarpa, and a few other banana trees are quite cold hardy, most will not tolerate extended freezing temperatures. Potted banana plants can be brought indoors to a bright, sunny room to spend the winter in a slowed active state. They can take up some space indoors, so you also can help them sleep through winter. As the weather cools, gradually reduce watering. Before the first frost, cut the plant to 6 inches in height and move it to a dark, cool location. Keep the soil just moist until the weather warms in the spring.

The stunning evergreen cordyline is hardy only in the warmest growing zones, but potted cordylines can be moved indoors when temperatures dip into the 60s. Place them in a spot with good ventilation and consistent indoor temperatures; avoid placing them near air vents or in drafty areas. Increase humidity around cordyline by situating it in a humid room or on a saucer filled with pebbles and water, and avoid fluoride-treated tap water. Although the plant does not require dormancy in winter, it does like a rest, so cut water some during fall and winter.

We’ll help you set up your first garden—whether that’s a few pots on your patio, a raised bed, or an in-ground plot out back—and select the right plants for your soil and region.
